LIFE  OF  ST.  CHARLES  BORROMEO. 


CHAPTER  I. 


ST.  CHARLES  AGAIN  MEETS  WITH  OPPOSITION  IX  HIS 
ECCLESIASTICAL  JURISDICTION. 


The  fame  of  the  saint's  charity  and  labours  during  the 
plague  spread  far  and  wide,  earning  for  him  acknow- 
ledgments from  distant  kings  and  princes,  and  dis- 
pelling the  calumnies  of  those  who  misinterpret  the 
actions  even  of  good  men.  A  certain  Cardinal,  having 
ad  occasion  to  observe  this,  said:  "The  Cardinal  of 
anta  Prassede  has  now  cleared  up,  once  for  all,  the 
doubts  of  those  who  chose  to  misunderstand  him,  for 
he  has  given  a  proof  they  cannot  gainsay  of  the  charity 
which  burns  in  his  heart,  by  putting  his  own  life  in 
jeopardy  for  the  sake  of  his  people."  Those  who 
entertained  ill-will  against  him — for  God  always  per- 
mits ill-will  against  the  just  in  order  to  try  their  virtue 
— were  now  put  to  silence,  and  even  when  they  would 

VOL.  IL  A 


2 


Life  of  St.  Charles  Borromeo. 


not  acknowledge  his  saintly  character,  there  remained 
nothing  which  they  could  take  hold  of  as  matter  for 
their  censures. 

There  was  a  fair  promise,  therefore,  that  out  of  the 
common  calamity  there  would  arise  an  era  of  peace 
and  forbearance ;  and  that  the  bickerings  about  ecclesi- 
astical jurisdiction,  which  even  yet  crippled  the  action 
of  the  Church  courts,  would  be  clean  forgotten.  So, 
indeed,  thought  all,  including  the  Crown  officers,  who 
deemed  that  this  was  the  least  return  they  could  make 
to  the  Cardinal  for  all  the  toil  and  anxiety  he  had 
undergone. 

But  the  enemy  of  mankind  was  excited  against  the 
servant  of  God  in  proportion  as  he  was  more  fully 
appreciated,  and  could  not  endure  that  he  should  be  left 
at  peace.  He  cast  about,  therefore,  to  set  up  some 
new  calumny  to  disturb  him,  if  that  were  possible. 
Such  is  the  lot  of  the  just  in  this  life,  as  it  is  written, 
"  Many  are  the  afflictions  of  the  just" 1  The  further 
a  man  advances  in  the  path  of  perfection,  the  greater 
are  the  obstacles  he  has  to  surmount,  in  proportion  as 
the  degree  of  glory  prepared  for  him  in  heaven  is 
also  greater.  The  saint  had  indeed  already  encoun- 
tered a  large  measure  of  suffering,  but  God  designed  to 
bestow  upon  him  a  brighter  crown,  and  therefore  per- 
mitted a  heavier  cross  to  be  laid  upon  him 

The  Governor  of  Milan  had  from  the  time  of  his 
accession  to  office  behaved  towards  the  Cardinal  with 
mistrust,  which  arose  no  doubt  from  the  fact  of  the 
excommunication  of  his  predecessor,  and  the  remon- 


Pi.  xxxiii.  20. 


Again  meets  with  Opposition.  3 


strances  he  had  brought  upon  himself  on  account  of 
his  absence  from  his  proper  sphere  of  duty.  Nor  were 
there  wanting  evil  counsellors  ever  ready  to  foster  ill- 
will  by  way  of  ingratiating  themselves.  There  were 
also  some  among  the  officers  of  the  Crown  who  bore 
malice  against  the  Cardinal  on  account  of  his  reforms, 
who  would  rather  have  been  left  in  their  old  evil  habits 
— his  saintly  example  being  a  thorn  in  their  side — 
as  is  said  in  the  Gospel,  "  He  who  walks  in  darkness 
hateth  the  light/' 1  Two  of  these  in  particular  were 
among  the  Governors  most  intimate  advisers,  and  bore 
an  especial  dislike  to  St.  Charles  because  he  had  on 
several  occasions  reproved  the  scandalous  license  of 
their  lives.  Yet  they  did  nothing  openly  against  him, 
but  cloaked  their  devices  under  a  show  of  zeal  for 
what  was  just  and  right,  in  which  they  succeeded  the 
better  that  one  of  them  had  formerly  been  intimate 
with  the  saint,  who  had  been  /  known  to  speak  of  him 
in  terms  of  commendation.  I  do  not  say  this  in  any 
way  to  vindicate  St  Charles,  whose  motives  no  one 
would  venture  to  call  in  question,  not  even  in  his  own 
day;  but  in  order  to  show  that  the  Governor  was 
really  deceived  in  his  opinion  of  the  man,  and  that 
the  opposition  arose  from  a  very  small  section  of  the 
King's  ministers,  the  great  majority  of  whom  were  right- 
minded  persons,  and  well  affected  towards  the  Cardinal, 
as  was  also  their  royal  master.  What  wonder  if  there 
were  some  who  were  ill-disposed  among  so  large  a 
number  of  upright  and  conscientious  persons,  seeing 
there  was  a  Judas  even  in  the  college  of  the  Apostles  ? 


1  John  iiL  20. 


4 


Life  of  St.  Charles  Borrovieo. 


The  city  had  hardly  been  declared  free  from  the 
contagion,  when  the  vexed  question  of  the  limits  of 
the  Archbishop's  jurisdiction  was  again  mooted  by 
the  Governor.  Matters  of  this  kind  relating  to  other 
dominions  of  the  Catholic  King  were  about  to  be 
submitted  to  the  judgment  of  the  Holy  See,  when 
the  Governor  seized  the  opportunity  of  opening  up 
his  suit.  In  pursuance  of  this  purpose  he  sent  an 
envoy  to  Rome  to  conduct  the  proceedings  in  his 
behalf,  little  doubting  the  cause  would  be  decided  in 
his  favour,  as  his  advisers  led  him  to  expect.  He 
selected  for  the  mission  a  certain  doctor,  whom  he 
knew  to  be  unfavourably  disposed  to  the  Cardinal's 
claims.  This  person  was  recommended  to  him  by 
the  two  adversaries  of  the  latter  already  mentioned, 
and  was,  in  fact,  their  creature.  To  his  commission 
they  superadded  instructions,  with  several  unfounded 
complaints  against  the  saint,  to  be  laid  before  the 
Sovereign  Pontiff,  wishing,  by  means  of  these  accusa-

to  obtain  the  readier  hearing  for  their  view  of  the 
question  of  jurisdiction,  and  above  all  to  neutralise 
his  power  of  enforcing  the  reforms  so  obnoxious  to 
them.  Among  other  things,  he  was  to  accuse  the 
Cardinal  of  having  endeavoured  to  exempt  ecclesi- 
astics from  the  observance  of  the  ordinances  made 
by  the  Governor  and  municipal  authorities  for  the 
regulation  of  the  city  during  the  pestilence,  alleging 
that  it  belonged  to  himself  to  give  orders  respecting 
the  quarantine  in  all  that  concerned  them.  Then 
he  was  to  pretend — though  there  was  no  foundation

whatever  for  the  allegation — that  great  mischief  had

counsellors  have  the  ear  of  a  ruler,  and  induce  him, 
under  the  plea  of  upholding  right,  to  do  all  manner 
of  injustice. 

But  this  was  not  all.  To  give  a  more  colourable 
appearance  to  their  inventions,  they  had  recourse  to 
the  base  artifice  of  representing  that  all  the  people 
of  Milan  were  aggrieved  by  the  restrictions  arbitrarily, 
as  they  alleged,  laid  by  the  Cardinal  upon  their 
liberties.  They  endeavoured  accordingly  to  obtain 
the  support  of  the  Council  of  the  city  for  their  com- 
plaints, but  it  was  only  a  very  slender  minority, 
misled  by  worldly  interests,  who  would  afford  them 
any  sanction,  and  the  whole  city  was  highly  indig- 
nant when  the  intrigue  was  made  public.  The  heads 
of  accusation  were,  that  he  had  prohibited  public 
amusements  and  balls  on  holidays,  allowing  nothing 
but  religion  to  be  then  attended  to;  that  he  had 
reserved  to  himself  the  sole  power  of  giving  absolu- 
tion for  a  great  number  of  sins;  that  he  had  abolished 
the  custom  of  allowing  the  use  of  meat  on  the  first 
Sunday  of  Lent ;  that  he  had  closed  up  all  the  side

entrances  of  the  churches,  and  revived  the  obsolete

It  would  seem,  however,  that,  with  all  their  malice, 
his  enemies  still  perceived  that  these  charges  were  at 
best  but  frivolous,  if  indeed  they  did  not  in  making 
them  run  the  risk  of  calling  attention  to  the  wisdom

find  something  more  tangible  to  lay  hold  to  his  pre-

inquisition  not  only  into  the  acts  of  the  Cardinal  him- 
self, but  also  into  those  of  his  rural  deans ;  and  sent 
for  the  deputies  of  many  towns  and  districts,  and 
examined  them,  in  many  cases  using  threats,  in  the 
hope  of  discovering  something  which  might  be  used

that  was  to  be  learnt  was  that  the  ministers  of  the 
Cardinal  were  diligent  in  their  duties  and  in  enforcing 
discipline.  Such  result,  instead  of  changing  their  pur- 
pose, was  received  by  them  only  with  disgust.

himself  of  another  expedient  Fancying  that  the 
reforms  the  Cardinal  had  so  vigorously  carried  out

Such  were  the  ways  in  which  the  emissary  of  the 
Governor  tried  to  bring  the  Cardinal  into  discredit. 
He  did  not  fail  to  urge  his  allegations  with  all  the 
address  he  could  command,  backing  them  with  the 
memorials  of  the  disaffected  religious,  and  not  hesitat-

too  frivolous  to  be  made  a  ground  of  serious  accusa- 
tion. But  the  Pontiff  was  not  thus  to  be  deceived. 
He  at  once  remarked  that  every  matter  of  complaint 
against  the  Archbishop  was,  rightly  considered,  deserv- 
ing of  praise,  and  tended  to  prove  his  wisdom  in  the 
government  of  his  diocese.  It  was  perfectly  clear, 
therefore,  that  the  whole  was  a  plot  of  the  enemy  of 
mankind  to  entrap  him,  an  outburst  of  his  malice 
against  St.  Charles  in  revenge  for  the  numbers  who 
had  been  delivered  from  his  snares  by  the  labours  of 
the  saint.  At  the  same  time  the  Holy  Father  was 
struck  with  indignation  that  any  persons,  calling  them- 
selves Christians,  should  have  been  found  to  listen  to 
such  suggestions  when  they  involved  so  great  an  in- 
justice towards  their  good  pastor ;  and  that  at  a  time 
when  he  had  been  ready  to  sacrifice  his  life  for  them, 
and  had  actually  spent  his  whole  energies  in  their  ser- 
vice, thus  rendering  him  cursing  instead  of  blessing — 
an  inconceivable  piece  of  ingratitude.  To  give  unmis- 
takable evidence  of  his  abhorrence  of  conduct  so  base, 
he  took  no  other  notice  of  the  charges  than  to  send  a 
statement  of  the  whole  matter  to  St.  Charles  himself, 
in  order  to  acquaint  him  with  the  sentiments  of  his 
flock — for  the  Pope  did  not  know  that  their  apparent 
concurrence  had  been  surreptitiously  obtained— and  that 
he  might  see  how  little  they  could  be  depended  upon. 

On  receiving  the  statement,  St.  Charles  was  not 
a  little  grieved  to  find  that  his  enemies  had  suffered 
themselves  to  be  caught  in  the  snares  of  Satan, 
and  lamented  the  scandals  that  might  result  from 
their  conduct,  as  well  as  the  dishonour  they  had

offered  to  God.  He  sent  for  some  of  the  principal

While  St.  Charles  was  content  to  take  no  steps 
to  vindicate  himself  from  the  charges  brought 
against  him,  he  was  far  from  passing  over  the 
matter  without  drawing  some  spiritual  profit  from  it. 
He  entertained  no  doubt  that  God  had  permitted  it 
for  a  good  purpose,  and  he  applied  himself  in  ear- 
nest to  learn  His  design.  He  called  to  mind  the 
examples  of  the  Apostles,  and  the  Bishops,  Ambrose, 
Basil,  John  Chrysostom,  and  others,  who,  in  doing 
their  duty,  and  in  asserting  the  authority  of  Holy 
Church,  bore  without  quailing  persecution,  exile,  and 
death.  Yet,  however  much  they  were  wronged,  they 
never  wearied  or  fainted  under  the  burden  laid  upon 
them,  but  laboured  more  strenuously  to  approve 
themselves  valiant  soldiers  of  Jesus  Christ,  the  cap- 
tain of  salvation.  These  considerations  strengthened 
him  to  advance  more  vigorously  in  the  path  of  reform, 
notwithstanding  the  disappointment  of  his  hopes,  the

door  opened  for  all  manner  of  evil  habits,  the  neglect 
of  the  decency  of  God's  service,  and  the  dishonour  done 
to  His  House,  leading  him  to  think  that  God  would 
punish  the  city  and  people  with  new  chastisement. 

In  the  midst  of  his  affliction  he  derived  consolation 
from  the  piety  of  the  Governor  s  wife,  who  being  her- 
self full  of  the  fear  of  God,  never  let  slip  any  oppor- 
tunity of  urging  her  husband  and  her  sons  to  remember 
the  respect  due  to  the  Archbishop,  and  to  observe  his 
precepts.  She  exerted  all  her  influence  also  to  get 
them  to  abstain  from  profane  diversions  on  festivals, 
in  which  certain  men  now  indulged,  on  purpose  to 
bid  defiance  to  the  saint.  Her  good  offices  availed 
little  more  than  the  fatherly  admonitions  of  the  Car- 
dinal himself  in  softening  their  hearts  and  turning 
them  to  obedience.  Though  all  else  failed,  he  con- 
tinued to  pray  for  them,  that  their  eyes  might  be 
opened  and  the  mist  of  passion  taken  away. 

To  his  prayers  he  added  increased  austerity  of  life, 
continuing  the  same  fasts  and  penances  which  he  had 
adopted  during  the  plague,  hoping  thus  to  obtain  grace 
for  his  persecutors.  When  Mgr.  Castello  of  Eimini, 
who  had  previously  been  his  Vicar-General,  besought 
him  to  moderate  this  rigour,  now  that  the  pestilence 
had  ceased,  he  replied,  with  humility,  "I  think  I 
ought  rather  to  increase  than  to  diminish  it,  since, 
though  the  plague  is  stayed,  the  cause  of  its  inflic- 
tion remains.  I  look  for  some  fresh  scourge  by  reason 
of  the  sins  and  offences  which  yet  abound  in  the

to  throw  in  his  way  were  thus  made  by  him  stepping- 
stones  to  a  higher  degree  of  perfection.  He  indeed 
never  rested,  but  when  he  had  carried  through  one 
measure  of  reform,  he  immediately  took  another  in 
hand. 

There  is  a  collegiate  church  in  Milan,  dedicated  to 
the  proto-martyr  St.  Stephen,  which  at  this  time  had 
but  six  Canons  and  a  Provost  in  residence,  with  but  a 
slender  stipend  for  their  maintenance.  Owing  to  this 
small  endowment  it  was  impossible  fittingly  to  cele- 
brate the  Divine  offices,  the  church  being  one  of  the 
most  spacious  as  well  as  the  most  ancient  in  the 
city,  and  the  Cardinal  was  accordingly  desirous  of 
increasing  the  revenues  and  the  number  of  Canons. 
During  the  visitation  he  had  noticed  another  collegiate 
church  of  St.  John  the  Evangelist,  at  Pontirolo,  on  the 
outskirts  of  his  diocese,  bordering  on  the  Venetian 
territory.  Pontirolo  was  a  straggling  village  of  no 
importance,  containing  only  a  few  scattered  dwellings, 
which  were  the  resort  of  outlaws  from  both  states. 
The  turbulence  of  these  men  kept  the  Canons  in  con- 
tinual peril  of  their  lives,  and  their  extortions  created 
great  scandal.  With  the  sanction  of  the  Holy  See 
and  the  consent  of  the  Canons,  he  transferred  this 
foundation  to  St.  Stephen's  at  Milan,  and  put  in  their 
place  a  secular  priest,  suppressing  three  canonries  in 
order  to  provide  him  with  a  sufficient  support.  There 
remained  twenty-four  prebends,  which  the  Cardinal 
reduced  to  eighteen,  that  there  might  be  a  proper 
maintenance  for  each.  To  these  he  added  a  theo- 
logical prebend,  thus  duly  providing  for  all  needs.  .

It  was  suggested  to  him  about  this  time  that  there 
were  relics  of  several  saints  in  different  parts  of  the 
cathedral  which  were  not  honoured  as  they  ought  to 
be.  There  were,  among  others,  the  body  of  St.  Diony- 
sius  Marianus,  twelfth  Bishop  of  Milan,  who  died  in 
exile  in  Further  Cappadocia,  whither  he  was  banished 
by  the  Emperor  Constantius,  the  abettor  of  the  Arian 
heresy ;  of  St.  Aurelius,  an  Armenian  Bishop,  who 
brought  to  Milan  the  body  of  St.  Dionysius  in  the 
time  of  St.  Ambrose ;  the  ashes  of  St.  Pelagia,  virgin 
and  martyr ;  and  some  of  the  bones  of  St.  Julian,  Bishop. 
St  Charles  collected  and  enclosed  them  in  proper 
shrines,  and  placed  them  in  the  crypt,  which  he  had 
previously  restored,  spending  a  great  part  of  the  day 
and  night  in  prayer  before  them.  At  the  same  time 
he  had  some  others,  viz.,  the  heads  of  St.  Maximus, 
martyr  of  the  Theban  legion ;  of  St  Thecla,  virgin  and 
martyr ;  of  St  Monas  and  Galdinus  della  Sala,  Car- 
dinal Priest  of  St  Sabina  and  Archbishop  of  Milan, 
placed  in  silver  shrines  that  they  might  be  exposed  for 
the  veneration  of  the  people  and  carried  in  processions. 

Among  abuses  which  he  set  himself  to  remedy  was 
the  want  of  reverence  among  the  people  for  holy 
places.  He  admonished  them  seriously  on  account  of 
the  disorders  which  often  happened  at  the  time  of  the 
indulgences,  and  issued  an  edict  requiring  that  men 
and  women  should  visit  the  churches  separately,  re- 
minding them  of  the  special  privilege  he  had  obtained 
for  them  from  Kome,  viz.,  the  indulgence  of  the  Seven 
Churches,  and  appointing  a  public  pilgrimage  to  them 
on  the  feast  of  the  Visitation  of  Our  Lady. 


14         Life  of  St.  Charles  Borromeo. 

On  this  occasion  he  wrote  a  pastoral  letter,  showing 
the  antiquity  of  these  stations,  the  object  for  which 
they  were  instituted,  the  value  of  the  indulgences 
attached  to  them,  and  the  importance  of  visiting  them ; 
exhorting  his  people  to  be  earnest  in  making  these 
visits,  and  to  treat  holy  places  with  veneration,  espe- 
cially on  account  of  the  Blessed  Sacrament  and  the 
precious  treasures  of  relics  which  they  contained. 

At  the  close  of  this  year  he  held  his  fifth  diocesan 
synod,  not  only  to  satisfy  the  obligation  of  his  office, 
but  also  to  have  an  opportunity  of  meeting  all  his 
clergy  together  after  the  afflictions  of  the  plague,  call- 
ing upon  them  for  signal  fruits  of  gratitude  for  their 
deliverance  in  the  salvation  of  souls.  This  synod 
sat  three  days,  and  on  each  day  he  addressed  the 
assembled  clergy  in  terms  more  moving  than  was 
usual  even  with  him.  On  the  last  day  in  particular 
he  spoke  of  the  obligations  of  the  parish  priests,  and 
denounced  the  negligence  of  those  who  are  wanting  in 
the  requirements  of  their  sacred  office.  The  eyes  of 
many  overflowed  with  tears  of  compunction,  and  that 
this  was  no  mere  passing  fervour  was  shown  by  the 
steady  resolution  that  was  taken  by  a  considerable 
number,  not  only  to  devote  themselves  more  seriously 
to  the  salvation  of  souls,  but  also  to  offer  themselves 
to  him  under  a  particular  obedience  in  the  Congrega- 
tion of  the  Oblates,  upon  the  foundation  of  which  he 
was  at  this  time  deliberating.  Many  wholesome  regu- 
lations were  laid  down  by  this  synod  for  the  further- 
ance of  his  reforms,  and  besides  these  public  labours 
he  found  time  to  grant  a  great  number  of  private

audiences,  finally  dismissing  the  clergy  much  edified

Another  measure  he  took  in  hand  was  to  induce 
the  Canons  of  the  metropolitan  church  to  unite  to- 
gether with  himself  in  a  community  life.  It  was 
his  perpetual  maxim  that  a  Bishop  was  bound  to 
aspire  to  nothing  less  than  apostolic  perfection;  he 
used  even  to  say  that  the  episcopal  order  presupposes 
a  state  of  more  eminent  holiness  than  that  of  cloistered 
religious.  This  was  always  his  guiding  principle,  and 
to  work  it  out  more  effectually  he  had  always  before 
his  eyes  the  example  of  some  Bishop  illustrious  for 
sanctity  in  the  Church  of  God,  as  a  model  and  guide 
for  all  his  actions.  Thus  he  was  always  striving  after 
the  attainment  of  more  and  more  perfection.  It  was 
with  this  intention  that  he  sought  to  revive  the  ancient 
custom 1  of  the  Bishop  living  in  community  with  his 
Canons.  A  season  of  rejoicing  for  the  cessation  of 
the  plague,  that  united  all  classes  in  a  common  bond, 
seemed  to  him  an  appropriate  time  to  join  again  in 
this  practice  of  fraternal  charity.  He  called  together 
the  Canons,  whom  he  always  regarded  as  his  brethren, 
and  opened  his  heart  to  them,  exhorting  them  to 
return  with  him  to  this  custom  of  the  early  Church, 
to  have  one  common  purse  as  brethren,  he  himself 
being  willing  to  lead  the  way.  He  showed  them 
that  it  was  in  perfect  conformity  with  their  name 
of  Canons,  which  implied  that  they  were  regular

While  the  whole  body  of  the  Chapter  concurred 
in  these  opinions,  a  small  number  only  offered  to 
adopt  them.  The  rest  thought  that  there  were  too 
many  obstacles  in  the  way  of  carrying  them  out,  and 
they  were  a  majority.  Eather  than  that  it  should 
lead  to  any  contention,  the  Cardinal  yielded,  recog- 
nising, as  was  his  wont  under  all  circumstances,  the 
hand  of  God  directing  him.  At  the  same  time  he 
was  too  well  convinced  of  the  benefit  such  an  ex- 
ample would  have  upon  the  rest  of  the  clergy  to  let 
the  matter  drop  altogether,  so  after  he  found  all 
endeavours  to  conform  the  opinions  of  the  present 
Canons  to  his  own  plans  unavailing,  he  determined 
to  found  a  new  congregation  of  priests,  and  to  give 
them  a  rule  of  common  life.

CHAPTER  III. 


THE  COMPANY  OF  THE  CROSSES  ;  COLLEGE  OF  SANTA 
SOPHIA  AND  THE  HOSPITAL  OF  MENDICANTS. 


We  have  already  spoken  of  the  altars  which  were 
erected  in  the  public  streets,  to  enable  the  people 
to  hear  Mass  during  the  time  they  were  kept  in 
their  houses  by  the  regulations  of  quarantine.  It 
would  seem  that  they  had  conceived  a  great  devotion 
towards  these  altars,  and  the  saint  thought  it  would 
be  a  means  of  perpetuating  their  gratitude  for  their 
deliverance  to  foster  this  feeling.  He  set  up,  therefore, 
in  those  places,  the  standard  of  the  Holy  Cross,  to 
keep  alive  a  perpetual  memory  of  the  Passion  of 
our  Lord,  and  to  fortify  the  city  in  every  part  with 
that  bulwark  of  our  salvation  against  the  assaults  of 
the  enemy;  to  make  Milan  a  religious  city,  signed 
on  every  side  with  the  sign  of  the  cross,  to  remind 
its  inhabitants  constantly  of  the  obligations  of  their 
calling  as  Christians.  He  had  crucifixes  placed  upon 
pedestals  of  stone,  with  an  iron  railing  to  preserve 
the  crosses  and  altars  to  which  they  were  attached, 
with  greater  reverence.  In  order  that  the  devotion 
vol.  n.  B 


1578. 


1 8  Life  of  St.  Charles  Borromeo. 


might  not  die  away,  he  instituted  a  company  or  con- 
fraternity of  pious  persons  of  the  neighbourhood  in 
which  each  crucifix  was  erected,  with  a  rule  and  offices 
of  their  own,  and  put  them  under  the  direction  of  the 
oblates  of  St.  Ambrose.  They  were  to  join  together 
every  evening  in  public  prayer  each  before  their  own 
crucifix,  and  to  go  in  procession  every  Friday  evening 
at  the  Ave  to  the  cathedral  to  visit  the  relic  of  tlie 
Holy  Nail,  and  assist  at  a  discourse  on  our  Lord's 
Passion. 

This  work  was  fruitful  in  benefits  to  souls,  parti- 
cularly in  the  treasures  of  indulgences  obtained  from 
the  Holy  See  for  its  members.  It  was  not,  however, 
suffered  by  Satan  to  flourish  without  opposition,  for 
the  King's  ministers  set  themselves  against  it  on  the 
plea  that  the  Cardinal  intended  to  exempt  all  these 
places  from  the  royal  jurisdiction,  but  they  did  not 
succeed  in  effecting  any  interruption  of  his  plans.  In 
saying  that  they  especially  promoted  the  glory  of  God 
we  need  only  mention  the  fact  of  so  large  a  number 
of  voices  being  raised  evening  by  evening  in  public 
thanksgiving  to  God  throughout  the  city,  of  so  many 
men  united  in  procession  every  Friday  to  honour  the 
Mysteries  of  the  Passion.  These  confraternities  are 
now  thirty-six  in  number  in  Milan  alone,  besides  those 
scattered  throughout  the  diocese,  and  twenty-five  other 
pious  associations  which  joined  them  in  their  religious 
exercises. 

Among  other  charitable  works  of  St.  Charles, 
during  the  time  of  the  plague,  of  which  we  have 
not  yet  spoken,  was  the  protectory  he  extended  over 


The  College  of  Santa  Sophia.  19 


young  girls,  who  being  left  orphans  and  destitute, 
stood  in  some  risk  of  losing  virtue  and  reputation. 
With  the  assistance  of  some  pious  persons,  and 
especially  of  a  member  of  the  Sant'  Agostino  family, 
a  conventual  father  of  the  Order  of  St  Francis,  he 
was  enabled  to  gather  them  all  into  a  place  of  safety. 
Though  the  pressure  of  the  terrible  time  was  past  he 
would  not  forsake  them,  but  resolved  to  open  a 
retreat  for  them,  where  they  might  be  safe  from  the 
perils  and  scandals  awaiting  them  in  the  world.  For 
this  purpose  he  hired  a  commodious  building,  with 
a  chapel  and  garden  attached,  called  St  Mary  of  the 
Angels,1  close  to  St  Calimero,  where  he  established 
them  under  the  invocation  of  the  Holy  Ghost  and 
title  of  Santa  Sophia,  committing  the  direction  of  the 
internal  affairs  of  the  house  to  the  Ursuline  nuns, 
and  its  temporal  concerns  to  a  Chapter  composed  of 
laymen  and  ecclesiastics,  who  governed  the  house 
according  to  a  rule  prescribed  by  the  saint.  This 
proved  one  of  the  greatest  benefits  conferred  by  him 
upon  the  city,  as  it  afforded  at  all  times  an  asylum 
for  poor  girls  exposed  to  temptation  in  the  world, 
from  which  they  were  not  only  preserved,  but,  more- 
over, brought  up  in  the  fear  of  God,  and  ultimately 
provided  for  in  good  situations  or  in  the  cloister, 
according  to  their  vocation. 

There  was  another  work  of  charity,  which  arose 
out  of  his  former  provision  for  the  plague-stricken. 
.We  have  before  spoken  of  the  place  of  refuge  he

gave  to  a  great  number  of  destitute  persons  in  the 
palace  of  Vittoria,  who,  now  that  the  danger  had 
passed  away,  expected  to  be  dispersed,  though  many 
of  them  had  lost  their  homes  and  their  all,  and  knew 
not  whither  to  go.  Their  pastor,  however,  could  not 
bear  to  send  them  away,  but  resolved  to  convert  this 
temporary  resort  into  a  permanent  hospital  for  mendi- 
cants of  both  sexes.  He  had  before  this  time  noticed 
the  wretched  condition  of  these  outcasts,  who  grew  up 
uninstructed  and  uncared  for,  driven  by  their  poverty 
to  gambling  and  stealing  and  all  manner  of  shameful 
modes  of  obtaining  their  livelihood,  besides  wandering 
about  the  churches  begging  and  distracting  people  at 
their  prayers,  and  that  others  were  led  to  join  them 
out  of  mere  idleness.  However  degraded  they  might 
be  in  the  world's  estimation,  to  his  eye  they  were 
souls  created  by  God  to  live  with  Him  in  Heaven, 
and  redeemed  by  the  precious  Blood  of  His  only  Son. 
The  Stella  convent,  in  the  suburb  of  the  Porta  Ver- 
cellina,  being  vacant,  he  fixed  upon  it  as  the  most 
convenient  place  for  these  outcasts,  as  it  not  only 
had  a  chapel  attached,  but  afforded  accommodation  for 
the  separation  of  the  sexes.  He  appointed  a  priest 
to  take  charge  of  their  spiritual  needs  and  to  instruct 
them,  and  nominated  a  committee  to  attend  to  their 
temporal  concerns,  contributing  largely  to  the  funds 
by  his  own  alms,  and  urging  others  to  do  the 
like.  He  obtained  from  the  Holy  See  a  Plenary 
Indulgence  for  Trinity  Sunday,  on  which  day  he 
instituted  a  special  procession  to  kindle  the  devotion 
of  the  people  more  abundantly  towards  this  hospital, 


Hospital  of  Mendicants.

and  to  induce  them  to  liberality  in  their  alms  for  its 
support.  By  his  rule,  all  destitute  persons,  whether 
natives  or  strangers,  were  admitted,  and  he  prevailed 
upon  the  public  authorities  thenceforward  to  prohibit 
begging  from  door  to  door  and  in  the  churches.

CHAPTER  IV. 

THE  VENERABLE  CONGREGATION  OF  THE  OBLATES  OF 
ST.  AMBROSE. 

I  573. 

Eighteen  years'  experience  hi  the  government  of  his 
See  had  taught  St.  Charles  the  impossibility  of  making 
the  progress  he  desired  in  establishing  discipline  and 
order  in  his  colleges,  seminaries,  and  other  foundations, 
without  the  assistance  of  efficient  ministers  and  fellow- 
workers,  who  being  disengaged  from  trammels  of  secu- 
lar affairs  should  be  free  to  carry  out  his  measures  for 
their  good  government.  The  dangers  to  which  those 
parts  of  his  diocese  that  bordered  on  heretical  states 
were  exposed,  urgently  called  for  such  a  body  of  men, 
as  did  also  the  want  of  priests  in  the  outlying  and 
mountainous  districts. 

To  supply  these  requirements  he  resolved  to  found 
a  congregation  of  secular  priests,  who  should  be  united 
under  himself  as  members  of  the  body  to  their  head, 
and  be  always  in  readiness  to  execute  promptly  what- 
ever work  he  appointed  them  to  do.  He  intended 
that  they  should  restore  a  perfect  pattern  of  ecclesias- 
tical discipline,  serving  God  purely  for  the  sake  of  His 


Digitized  by 


Congregation  of  Oblates  of  St.  Ambrose.  23 

glory  without  seeking  their  own  interest,  and  living 
together  in  common  as  brethren  in  the  Lord. 

Having  taken  counsel  with  God  in  prayer,  according 
to  his  wont,  he  made  choice  of  certain  ecclesiastics 
who  appeared  to  him  most  fitted  for  his  new  institute, 
out  of  those  who  had  offered  themselves  after  his  dis- 
course at  the  last  Synod.  Having  thus  got  together  a 
good  number,  he  laid  the  foundation  of  his  new  con- 
gregation on  the  1 6th  of  August,  1578,  the  feast  of 
St.  Simplicianus,  Archbishop  of  Milan,  and  placed  it 
under  the  protection  of  our  Blessed  Lady  and  St. 
Ambrose,  Doctor  of  the  church  and  patron  of  the  city, 
giving  it  the  title  of  the  Congregation  of  the  Oblates 
of  St.  Ambrose.  It  afterwards  received  the  approval 
and  confirmation  of  the  Supreme  Pontiff  Gregory 
XIII.,  who  granted  to  it  privileges  of  indulgences  in 
perpetuity,  and  some  ecclesiastical  revenues  remaining 
over  from  the  suppressed  Order  of  the  Frati  Humiliati. 
St  Charles  assigned  for  its  first  establishment  the 
Church  of  the  Holy  Sepulcre,  which  had  belonged  to 
some  titular  Canons,  who  had  long  ceased  to  reside 
there,  together  with  some  adjoining  houses  which  he 
bought  of  the  pious  Society  of  the  Eosary,  which 
afforded  all  the  means  for  the  exercise  of  their  ministry. 
He  made  choice  of  this  place  because  it  was  situated 
in  the  very  heart  of  the  city — a  convenient  base  of 
operations  for  all  parts — and  because  it  was  much 
frequented  by  the  people  out  of  devotion  to  the  Holy 
Sepulcre  and  other  mysteries  of  the  Passion,  which 
were  there  commemorated  in  sculpture.  It  had  always 
been  the  custom  to  have  priests  at  this  church  to  say

24 


Life  of  St.  Charles  Borromeo. 


the  Rosary,  visit  the  sick  poor,  and  employ  themselves 
in  the  work  of  souls. 

When  St  Charles  first  came  to  Milan,  he  found  at 
this  church  Father  Gaspar  Belinzago,  and  others  with 
him,  whose  zeal  and  devotion  in  the  service  of  God 
might  be  said  to  have  kept  alive  the  light  of  faith  at 
a  time  when  piety  was  at  a  low  ebb  in  the  city.  This 
Father  had  been  called  to  a  better  life  about  three  years 
before  the  foundation  of  St.  Charles'  institute,  amid 
the  regrets  of  all  the  people,  who  held  him  for  a  saint. 
Some  of  his  priests  joined  the  new  congregation,  among 
whom  was  Father  Francis  Crippa,  a  man  of  apostolic 
spirit,  greatly  esteemed  for  his  sanctity,  who  was  the 
confessor  of  Ludovico  Moneta.  The  spirit  of  primitive 
piety  which  animated  this  little  band  of  priests  had 
no  small  share  in  St.  Charles'  selection  of  their  house, 
as  he  himself  bears  testimony  in  the  constitutions  of 
this  congregation,  by  saying  that  he  hoped  it  would 
be  hereditary  in  their  house  and  perpetually  kept  up 
among  them.  > 

The  rule  which  he  gave  them  is  to  be  found  at 
length  in  the  "  Acts  of  the  Church  of  Milan."  The 
leading  features  of  it  are  that  the  oblates  should  be 
under  the  obedience  of  the  Archbishop,  taking  the 
simple  vow  of  obedience  at  his  hands  on  entering  the 
congregation :  that  they  should  be  united  to  him  as 
the  members  of  a  body  to  their  head,  sharing  in  his 
spirit,  his  zeal,  and  his  desire  for  the  glory  of  God  and 
the  salvation  of  souls :  that  they  should  in  all  their 
actions  breathe  a  spirit  of  piety,  and  aim  at  that  reli- 
gious perfection  which  should  prove  them  worthy  of 


Congregation  of  Oblates  of  St.  A  mbrose.    2  5 


such  a  union.  It  should  be  their  especial  office  to  aid 
the  Archbishop  in  the  government  of  his  diocese,  and 
to  co-operate  with  him  in  all  his  functions  and  offices, 
and  particularly  in  his  visitations.  They  should  be 
ready  at  all  times  to  go  out  like  apostle3  upon  any 
mission  which  he  might  entrust  to  them,  especially  in 
places  which,  on  account  of  their  remoteness  and  in- 
accessibility, were  often  left  destitute  of  spiritual  aids ; 
also  to  take  temporary  care  of  parishes  during  vacan- 
cies, to  discharge  the  duties  of  urban  inspectors  or 
rural  deans :  to  direct  colleges,  seminaries,  schools  of 
Christian  doctrine,  Confraternities  of  the  Cross,  to 
give  the  spiritual  exercises  to  those  preparing  for  Holy 
Orders,  and  in  general  to  be  ready  to  preach,  administer 
the  sacraments,  and  undertake  other  pious  works  to 
which  they  might  be  called.  He  directed  that  all 
the  devotions  which  were  usual  at  Santa  Maria  in 
Vallicella,  the  Church  of  the  Oratory  in  Home,  should 
also  be  practised  at  the  Church  of  the  Holy  Sepulcre : 
a  custom  which  was  very  advantageous  in  gaining 
souls  and  giving  pious  occupation  to  many  persons 
who  had  leisure. 

All  these  intentions  were  fully  carried  out,  and  we 
see  at  this  day  more  than  two  hundred  priests  belong- 
ing to  this  institute ;  many  with  the  degree  of  Doctor 
in  Theology,  and  all  of  singular  holiness  of  life, 
their  united  labours  working  great  benefits  in  the 
diocese.  We  cannot  be  far  wrong,  therefore,  in  reckon- 
ing this  work  among  the  labours  of  the  saint  that  were 
greatly  blessed  in  the  spiritual  vineyard  of  the  Church. 

He  divided  the  oblates  into  two  classes.    The  first 


26         Life  of  St.  Charles  Borromeo. 

were  to  remain  permanently  at  St.  Sepulcre's  without 
holding  any  cure  which  bound  them  to  residence,  so 
that  they  might  be  free  to  exercise  any  ministry  that 
might  be  required  of  them.  Those  of  the  second 
order  were  to  be  distributed  in  different  parishes  of 
the  city  or  diocese,  and  bound  to  residence. 

Though  they  were  by  this  arrangement  sometimes 
separated  from  one  another,  in  order  to  keep  them  united 
in  spirit,  so  that  they  should  all  feel  themselves  part 
of  the  body,  keep  alive  the  spirit  of  the  institute, 
and  grow  continually  in  virtue,  he  divided  the  con- 
gregation into  six  consortia  or  companies,  two  being 
established  in  the  city,  and  four  in  other  parts  of  the 
diocese,  to  each  of  which  he  gave  a  Superior  and  a 
spiritual  Prefect  Each  of  the  companies  were  to  meet 
once  a  month,  those  in  the  city  at  St.  Sepulcre's  in 
presence  of  the  Archbishop,  those  in  other  parts  of  the 
diocese,  sometimes  in  one  place,  sometimes  in  another, 
presided  over  by  the  Superior-general,  or  at  least  by 
the  Superior  of  the  particular  company.  These  associa- 
tions were  to  be  opened  by  reading  the  rule  of  the 
congregation,  after  which  the  members  were  to  confer 
upon  the  mode  of  its  observance,  upon  their  progress 
in  the  spiritual  life,  and  upon  the  means  of  advancing 
souls  in  the  way  of  salvation.  The  president  was  to 
exhort  them  to  perfection,  and  two  members  of  the 
congregation  were  to  preach  in  public  to  the  people 
on  some  profitable  topic.  This  practice  not  only  kept 
up  a  spirit  of  union  and  brotherly  love  among  all 
the  members,  but  afforded  a  means  of  continually 
infusing  into  them  anew  the  mind  and  intention  of 


Digitized  by 


Congregation  of  Oblates  of  St.  Ambrose.  27 


their  head,  the  Archbishop,  so  as  to  reproduce  and 
multiply  his  efforts  for  the  benefit  of  the  souls  of  his 
people  in  every  part  of  his  diocese. 

The  love  which  he  bore  to  the  oblates  was  very 
manifest,  for  he  always  called  them  his  sons,  and 
treated  them  as  such.  He  chose  out  a  little  cell  at 
St  Sepulcre's,  where  he  often  went  to  stay  with  them, 
and  behaved  with  such  humility  as  if  he  had  been  one 
of  the  least  of  them,  following  all  the  observances  of 
the  house.  He  was  always  pleased  to  be  there,  and 
spoke  of  it  as  one  of  his  greatest  enjoyments,  and  used 
to  say  that  it  ought  to  be  the  special  recreation  of  an 
Archbishop  of  Milan.  If  any  of  them  fell  ill,  he  was 
not  content  with  simply  visiting  them,  but  would 
attend  upon  them  himself  with  every  sign  of  the 
lively  interest  he  took  in  their  well-being.  In  the 
year  1580,  a  priest  of  the  house  named  John  Peter 
Stoppano,  at  the  present  time  archpriest  of  Mazzo  in  the 
Valtellina,  was  seized  with  a  mortal  sickness.  When 
the  saint  heard  of  it,  he  went  to  see  him  without  loss 
of  time,  and  installed  himself  at  the  bedside  of  the 
dying  man,  attending  him  by  day  and  by  night,  as  if 
he  had  been  infirmarian,  through  all  the  crisis  of  his 
sickness,  till  it  had  reached  the  last  stage,  and  he 
seemed  about  to  deliver  up  his  soul  to  his  Maker. 
But  the  saint  who  foresaw  keenly  the  loss  which  the 
death  of  such  a  priest  would  prove  to  the  diocese, 
besought  God  for  his  recovery  so  earnestly  that  he 
obtained  it  When  great  surprise  at  this  cure  was 
shown,  "  You  do  not  know,"  he  said,  "  the  value  of  the 
life  of  a  good  priest." 


28         Life  of  St.  CJiarles  Borromeo. 


It  was  part  of  the  design  of  St.  Charles  to  found 
other  houses  of  his  congregation  in  all  the  principal 
cities  and  towns  of  his  diocese,  similar  to  that  of  St. 
Sepulcre,  as  we  see  by  the  rule  which  provides  that 
a  number  of  the  oblates  should  be  in  readiness  to  be 
sent  to  other  places,  to  act  as  eyes,  by  which  he  might 
learn  the  wants  and  necessities  of  his  flock.  He  was 
prevented,  however,  by  death,  from  carrying  out  this 
extension  of  the  institute;  but  he  annexed  to  it  a 
congregation  of  laymen,  and  gave  them  a  rule  of 
their  own.  They  were,  while  continuing  to  live  in 
their  own  homes,  to  occupy  themselves  in  good  works, 
particularly  in  giving  instruction  in  Christian  doc- 
trine. Besides  this,  he  instituted  a  congregation  of 
matrons,  also  attached  to  the  church  of  the  Holy 
Sepulcre,  with  the  title  of  Company  of  the  Ladies  of 
the  Oratory,  for  whose  guidance  he  prescribed  rules 
and  works  of  piety.  He  endeavoured  to  enlist  in 
this  band  the  ladies  of  the  principal  families  of  the 
city,  who  otherwise  would  be  likely  to  spend  their 
time  in  vain  amusements  and  other  evils  of  idleness. 
He  wished  thus  to  lead  them  to  frequent  the  Sacra- 
ments, to  attend  the  sermons  and  to  keep  alive  in  their 
minds  the  Passion  of  our  Divine  Eedeemer.

CHAPTER  V. 


HLGRDIAGE  TO  THE  HOLY  WINDING-SHEET  AT  TURIN. 


The  Passion  of  our  Divine  Lord  might  be  said  to  have 
been  the  particular  devotion  of  our  saint.  Thus  he 
cherished  a  great  reverence  for  all  its  sacred  instru- 
ments, as  we  have  seen  in  the  case  of  the  Holy  Nail. 
He  had  often  expressed  a  desire  to  visit  the  Holy 
Winding-sheet,  in  which  the  sacred  body  of  our  Lord 
reposed  in  the  sepulchre.  When  he  saw  his  people 
wasted  by  the  pestilence,  he  resolved  to  make  a  pil- 
grimage to  the  place  where  it  was  preserved,  in  order 
to  beg  God  to  have  mercy  on  his  flock. 

This  precious  relic  of  the  winding-sheet  of  our 
Lord  is  preserved  at  Chambery,  in  Savoy,  where  it 
was  held  in  great  honour  by  the  dukes  of  that  pro- 
vince, w"ho  watched  over  it  as  a  precious  heirloom 
entrusted  by  the  hand  of  God  to  the  keeping  of  their 
house.  It  was  brought  from  Jerusalem  in  the  crusade 
in  which  Godfrey  de  Bouillon  was  made  King  of 
Jerusalem,  and  was  held  for  many  generations  in  the 
family  of  the  Lusignans,  Bangs  of  Cyprus.  In  pro- 
cess of  time  it  came  into  the  hands  of  Margaret 


1573. 


3<D         Life  of  St.  Charles  Borromeo. 

Carma,  wife  of  Hector  Lusignan,  who  took  refuge  in 
France  when  the  Turks  overran  Greece  in  1457. 
She  travelled  safely  as  far  as  Chamber)',  which  was  at 
that  date  the  residence  of  the  Dukes  of  Savoy,  and 
was  affectionately  received  by  the  reigning  Duke, 
Louis,  and  Anna  Lusignan  his  wife,  herself  a  sister 
of  John  the  last  King  of  Cyprus,  and  a  relative  of 
Margaret.  During  her  stay  in  that  city,  God  was 
pleased  to  show  by  miracles  that  this  was  the  very 
winding-sheet  of  our  Saviour,  upon  which  the  Duchess 
Anna  was  moved  with  so  great  a  devotion  towards  it, 
that  she  earnestly  entreated  her  cousin  to  make  her 
a  present  of  the  treasure.  But  Margaret,  whose 
veneration  for  it  was  no  less  sincere,  replied  that  she 
would  rather  part  with  everything  she  possessed  in 
the  world  than  with  this,  and  soon  afterwards  set 
out  on  her  journey  northwards. 

The  devotion  of  the  Duchess  Anna  was,  however,  to 
have  its  reward,  as  the  relic  she  so  ardently  desired  at 
last  came  into  her  hands.  For  Margaret  had  hardly 
reached  the  outskirts  of  the  city  when  it  was  found 
that  the  mule  which  carried  it  could  not  be  made  to 
go  on,  though  beaten  with  many  stripes.  Margaret 
took  this  as  a  manifestation  that  the  relic  was  to 
remain  in  the  custody  of  her  relatives,  and  consigned 
it  accordingly  to  their  keeping.  The  Duke  and  his 
consort,  not  wanting  in  gratitude  for  this  favour,  with 
public  prayers  and  processions,  laid  it  up  in  a  chapel 
of  their  palace  prepared  to  receive  it,  and  erected  into 
a  collegiate  church  by  Pope  Paul  II. 

The  relic  continued  for  many  years  to  attract  the

veneration  of  the  faithful,  many  of  whom,  including 
kings  and  princes,  made  pilgrimages  to  visit  it. 
Among  the  rest  came  Francis  I.  of  France.  This 
prince  being  in  danger  of  defeat  from  the  Swiss  forces 
at  Melegnano,  about  eight  miles  from  Milan,  made  a 
vow  that  if  he  should  gain  the  victory,  he  would  make 
a  pilgrimage  to  the  holy  relic.  Immediately  the  day 
turned  in  his  favour,  and  though  his  army  was  well- 
nigh  cut  to  pieces,  he  was  left  master  of  the  field,  on 
the  15  th  June,  1516.  He  withdrew  soon  after  to 
Lyons,  and  then,  in  accomplishment  of  his  vow,  went 
on  foot  to  Chambery,  to  venerate  the  relic,  conceiving 
at  the  same  time  a  great  desire  to  possess  it.  This 
came  to  be  so  well  known,  that  when  he  was  engaged 
in  hostilities  with  the  Duke  of  Savoy,  fourteen  yeais 
later,  it  was  removed  for  safety  to  Vercelli  in  Pied- 
mont. In  the  reign  of  Francis's  son,  Henry  II.,  who 
inherited  his  father's  desire,  when  in  November,  1553, 
war  was  waged  in  Piedmont,  Brissac,  the  commander, 
thought  he  could  not  carry  back  a  more  acceptable 
trophy  to  the  King  than  the  holy  winding-sheet ;  but 
after  making  his  way  to  the  place  where  it  was  kept, 
he  was  miraculously  impeded  from  advancing  beyond 
the  threshold,  and  forced  to  retire.  When  peace  was 
restored  the  relic  was  brought  back  to  Chambery  by 
Duke  Emanuel  Philibert  in  1560. 

To  return  to  our  history.  The  Cardinal  resolved 
when  his  diocese  was  free  from  pestilence  to  fulfil  his 
intention  of  visiting  Chambery  in  order  to  render 
thanks  for  this  great  mercy  before  the  precious  relic. 
He  determined  to  make  the  journey  on  foot,  though

he  had  to  cross  difficult  passes  through  the  moun-

deposited.  He  then  sent  his  secretary,  Francis  Lino,

him  to  take  up  his  quarters  in  his  palace,  in  order  that

After  concluding  a  league  with  the  Swiss  ambas-

choosing  twelve  members  of  his  household  to  accom- 
pany him,  together  with  Father  Francesco  Adorno,  S.J., 
to  give  the  spiritual  exercises  during  the  journey. 
The  day  before  they  set  out,  he  assembled  all  the 
pilgrims  in  his  private  chapel,  and  one  of  their  number 
addressed  the  rest  in  presence  of  the  whole  household 
upon  two  points,  viz. :  devotion  towards  the  holy  relic 
they  were  going  to  visit,  and  penance  for  their  sins, 
exhorting  them  to  suffer  no  other  thoughts  to  occupy 
their  minds.

A  time-table  was  drawn  up  for  the  pilgrims  that  all 
things  might  be  done  to  edification.  They  were  to 
rise  every  morning  at  four  o'clock,  each  priest  was  to 
say  Mass,  and  the  pthers  were  to  go  to  communion  at 
the  Cardinal's  Mass,  and  say  the  offices  of  prime  and 
terce ;  they  were  then  to  begin  the  days  journey,  re- 
peating the  Itinerary,  then  two  hours  of  mental  prayer, 
and  the  Rosary  aloud  with  a  meditation  on  each 
mystery.  If  there  should  be  any  more  time  left 
before  they  reached  the  next  halting-place,  it  was  to 
be  spent  in  saying  certain  psalms  and  in  spiritual  con- 
versation. On  their  arrival  at  the  place  when  they 
were  to  rest,  they  were  to  go  at  once  to  the  church, 
and  after  spending  some  time  in  prayer,  to  say  sext 
and  none  on  their  knees,  and  then  take  their  refection, 
which  consisted  of  Lenten  fare.  While  they  were 
at  table,  a  spiritual  book  was  read.  Afterwards  they 
made  a  visit  to  the  church  to  make  a  thanksgiving 
and  say  vespers,  and  then  continued  their  journey, 
giving  two  hours  to  mental  prayer  and  reciting  the 
penitential  psalms  and  other  devotions  to  fill  up  the 
time,  no  part  of  which  was  without  its  proper  occupa- 
tion. In  the  evening  when  they  arrived  at  the  place 
where  they  were  to  pass  the  night,  they  went  to  the 
church  and  said  compline.  After  the  evening  refec- 
tion they  met  again  for  a  spiritual  conference  upon  the 
meditations  of  the'  past  day,  and  Father  Adorno  gave 
out  the  points  for  the  following  day.  Then  after  a 
quarter  of  an  hour's  examination  of  conscience,  the 
Cardinal  sprinkled  them  with  holy  water,  and  they

withdrew  for  the  night,  each  saying  matins  by  himself 
at  his  own  convenience. 

The  meditations  were  arranged  with  the  same  fore- 
thought The  distance  between  Milan  and  Turin  is 
about  ninety  miles,  and  it  was  divided  into  four  days' 
journey.  The  meditation  of  the  first  day  was  upon 
the  pilgrimage  of  our  Divine  Lord  through  this  world, 
while  He  was  preaching  the  Gospel,  healing  the  sick, 
and  delivering  souls  from  the  bondage  of  sin.  That 
of  the  second  day,  upon  the  pilgrimage  sufferings  and 
persecutions  of  the  apostles ;  on  the  third  day,  the 
pilgrimage  of  poor  mortal  men  through  this  world ;  on 
the  fourth,  the  proper  way  of  adoring  the  holy  Winding- 
sheet,  and  the  edification  to  be  derived  from  contem- 
plating the  marks  of  those  wounds  which  the  Son  of 
God  endured  for  our  salvation. 

They  set  out  from  Milan  on  the  6th  October,  1578, 
which  was  a  Monday.  Early  that  morning  all  the 
pilgrims  assembled  in  their  habit  in  chapel,  where 
the  saint  said  Mass,  and  gave  communion  to  all  who 
were  not  priests,  as  they  each  said  their  own  Mass. 
Vested  in  full  pontificals,  he  gave  them  his  benedic- 
tion, and  a  pilgrim's  staff  to  each.  They  went  to  the 
city  gate  in  procession  two  by  two,  the  Chapter  of  the 
cathedral  accompanying  them,  and  the  Cardinal,  at- 
tended by  a  great  number  of  the  clergy  and  people, 
bringing  up  the  rear,  all  singing  the  Gradual  psalms. 
On  arriving  at  the  Porta  Vercellina,  leading  to  Ver- 
celli,  the  Cardinal  put  on  his  purple  habit,  in  accord- 
ance with  the  pilgrim's  character,  with  the  rochet  and 
mantelletta  over  it    He  then  embraced  his  Canons

with  great  affection,  receiving  from  them  the  kiss  of

arranged,  and  continued  his  journey  through  the

When  he  rose  from  his  knees,  the  Duke  led  him  to  his

It  pleased  God  to  try  His  holy  servant  in  this  way, 
and  suffer  him  to  be  treated  with  this  external  show. 
We  must  not  imagine  that  these  things  afforded  him 
in  themselves  any  gratification.  He  would  have 
reckoned  himself  to  be  better  served,  had  he  been 
in  a  poor  hut,  than  surrounded  with  all  the  state  and 
pageant  of  the  palace.  A  scanty  repast  of  herbs  would 
have  been  more  to  his  taste  than  the  costly  viands 
placed  before  him.  But  while  he  felt  no  complacency, 
he  knew  how  to  gain  both  pleasure  and  profit  from 
them,  taking  them  as  the  simple  expression  of  an 
affectionate  disposition  on  the  part  of  the  Prince,  in 
order  to  converse  upon  matters  which  he  dexterously 
improved  to  his  spiritual  benefit,  for  he  knew  that 
those  in  high  station  do  not  often  find  any  to  advise 
them  in  such  way.  But  our  Lord  was  pleased  to 
grant  him  a  favour,  which  was  far  more  to  his  mind, 
as  it  gave  him  the  opportunity  of  doing  penance  for  His 
sake,  viz.,  great  suffering  in  one  foot  The  many  miles 
of  bad  roads  he  had  traversed  had  caused  blisters  on 
the  soles  of  his  feet,  and  in  having  them  cut  by 
an  unskilful  barber,  he  received  a  severe  wound  which 
took  many  days  to  heaL  He  endured  this  suffering 
with  fortitude,  and  did  not  omit  any  of  his  visits 
to  the  churches  or  other  necessary  walking,  notwith- 
standing the  pain  it  caused  him.  It  was  indeed 
to  him  a  cause  of  rejoicing,  as  it  gave  him  an  oppor- 
tunity of  tasting  some  of  the  sufferings  endured  by 
our  Divine  Kedeemer,  which  were  brought  to  his 
mind  by  the  contemplation  of  the  linen  cloth,  which 
had  received  the  impress  of  His  most  sacred  wounds,

His  precious  blood,  and  the  whole  of  His  suffering

and  said  Mass,  surrounded  by  a  great  concourse  of 
people,  who  came  to  hear  it  and  receive  communion 
at  his  hands.  Afterwards  the  Duke  expressed  a  wish

The  pilgrims  could  not  restrain  their  tears  as  they 
gazed  upon  the  precious  memorial  of  the  sufferings  of 
the  Son  of  God,  and  traced  out  the  marks  where  the 
thorns  had  pierced  His  Sacred  Head,  and  where  the 
spitting  had  defiled  His  Divine  Countenance,  where  the 
nails  had  torn  His  hands  and  feet,  and  the  lance 
entered  into  His  side,  and  blows  and  bruises  lacerated 
His  body  in  every  part.  The  saint  did  not  rest  satis- 
fied with  this  outward  adoration,  but  entered  into  the 
depths  of  woe  which  overwhelmed  the  Sacred  Heart  of 
Jesus,  of  which  these  were  but  the  tokens.  This 
contemplation  awakened  his  tenderest  sympathy,  and 
though  he  took  great  pains  to  conceal  his  emotion,  he 
could  not  prevent  his  tears  from  falling  and  bearing 
witness  how  those  sufferings  were  graven  on  his  heart.

Before  he  left  the  church,  the  relic  being  so  con- 
veniently placed,  he  satisfied  his  devotion  to  the  full 
by  kissing  it,  and  particularly  the  marks  of  the  sacred 
wounds. 

On  the  following  morning  he  again  visited  it  at 
San  Lorenzo,  whither  it  had  been  taken,  said  his 
Mass,  and  remained  some  time  in  prayer  before  it. 
He  asked  the  young  Prince  Charles  to  dine  with  him 
that  day,  and  had  the  Bible  read,  while  they  were 
at  table,  according  to  his  custom.  He  took  occasion 
from  the  part  of  Holy  Scripture  they  had  read,  viz.,  the 
Book  of  Macchabees,  to  enter  into  conversation  with 
the  Prince,  and  was  glad  to  find  him  well  acquainted 
with  the  Sacred  Scriptures,  so  that  he  formed  a  high 
opinion  of  his  understanding,  and  entertained  much 
affection  for  him.  It  was  then  arranged  that 
the  relic  should  be  carried  in  procession  to  the 
cathedral  the  next  morning,  that  it  might  be  seen  by 
the  people,  and  a  station  of  forty  hours'  devotion 
observed  before  it,  according  to  the  Milanese  use, 
also  that  the  saint  should  sing  the  Mass,  and  preach. 
It  was  found,  however,  that  the  function  attracted 
such  crowds  of  people  from  distant  parts  that  the 
cathedral  could  not  hold  them  alL  It  was,  therefore, 
agreed  to  adjourn  to  the  Piazza  del  Castello,  a 
spacious  place,  where  all  could  see  it  easily.  A  plat- 
form was  erected  there,  and  early  in  the  morning 
the  relic  was  transported  thither  in  state,  accom- 
panied by  the  two  Cardinals,  the  Archbishop  of  Turin, 
Joseph  Parpaglia,  Archbishop  of  Tarantasia,  and  six

Bishops,1  preceded  by  the  clergy,  the  Duke,  Ottavio

Prince  Charles,  the  orders  of  knights,  and  the  people. 

As  soon  as  the  Cardinals  and  Archbishops  had

Body  of  our  Lord.  It  was  a  sight  so  moving  that 
the  whole  assemblage,  at  the  spectacle  of  what  the 
Son  of  God  had  suffered  for  them,  rent  the  air  with 
cries  of  sorrow  and  contrition. 

It  was  then  conveyed  to  the  cathedral,  where  it 
was  laid  in  an  elevated  place  in  the  sight  of  the 
people,  and  a  station  of  forty  hours'  devotion  begun ; 
the  clergy  and  people  from  all  parts  keeping  up  the 
watch  by  night  and  day,  the  knights  of  St  Maurice 
and  St  Lazarus,  in  the  robes  of  their  order,  assisting. 
Every  hour  a  discourse  was  addressed  to  the  people, 
three  of  which  fell  to  the  share  of  the  saint,  one  to 
the  Cardinal  of  Vercelli,  others  to  the  Bishops  who 
had  taken  part  in  the  function,  and  the  remainder 
to  the  theologians  and  regular  clergy  of  the  city. 
The  Duke  and  his  son  set  an  example  of  devotion; 
as  they  not  only  often  visited  the  relic,  but  were 
more  than  once  seen  in  tears.  During  this  station 
St  Charles  went  to  visit  the  bodies  of  the  holy 
martyrs,  Solutor,  Adventor,  and  Octavius,  citizens  of

staying  the  further  progress  of  heresy. 

Having  now  accomplished  all  the  objects  he  had  in

him.  When  the  hour  for  his  departure  came,  he

CHAPTER  VI. 


VISIT  TO  MONTE  DI  VARALLO — PRAYERS  FOR  PHILIP  II., 


The  contemplation  of  the  relic  he  had  visited  left  upon 
the  mind  of  the  saint  so  lively  a  sympathy  for  the 
sufferings  of  our  Lord  that  he  resolved,  before  return- 
ing to  Milan,  to  visit  the  holy  mountain  of  Varallo  to 
meditate  in  private  on  the  mysteries  of  the  Passion, 
commemorated  there  in  little  chapels  distributed  over 
the  mountain. 

Having  taken  leave  of  the  Duke,  who  accompanied 
him  a  considerable  distance  on  his  way,  he  set  out  for 
this  place,  taking  with  him  only  six  of  his  companions 
and  Father  Adorno  his  confessor.  He  was  accom- 
panied also  by  the  Cardinal  of  Vercelli,  as  he  wished 
to  visit  on  his  way  the  relics  of  the  saints  preserved  at 
the  Abbey  of  St  Michael,  belonging  to  the  latter.  He 
said  Mass  there  and  passed  the  greater  part  of  the  day 
in  prayer  before  them,  continuing  his  journey  the  next 
morning. 

Varallo  is  situated  in  the  diocese  of  Novara,  in  the 
valley  of  Sesia,  bordering  on  Switzerland.    About  a

47 


hundred  years  before,  a  Franciscan  Father,  a  native  of 
Milan,  of  the  noble  family  of  the  Caimi,  had  built  a 
church  in  honour  of  our  Lady  on  one  of  the  lofty  peaks 
of  this  district,  and  many  little  chapels  dedicated  to  the 
mysteries  of  the  Life  and  Passion  of  our  Divine  Lord, 
one  of  which  was  copied  from  the  Holy  Sepulcre  at 
Jerusalem,  which  the  father  had  visited.  The  site  was 
retired  from  the  noise  and  turmoil  of  the  world,  while 
in  itself  it  was  picturesque  and  well  adapted  for  the 
purpose  of  holy  contemplation.  The  princifml  mystery 
gives  it  the  general  name  of  the  Sepulcre  of  Varallo, 
but  beside  the  large  church,  which  was  served  by 
Franciscan  friars,  there  are  thirty-eight  chapels  where 
are  portrayed  all  the  mysteries  of  the  Life,  Death,  and 
Eesurrection  of  our  Saviour  in  figures  of  the  size  of 
life,  embellished  with  paintings.  Its  first  founder  had 
moreover  enriched  it  by  a  number  of  precious  relics. 

It  was  two  o'clock  in  the  day  before  St.  Charles 
arrived  at  this  place,  and  he  had  not  broken  his  fast, 
but  before  taking  anything  he  visited  the  different 
chapels  for  meditation,  of  which  Father  Adorno  gave 
him  the  points.  As  evening  drew  on,  he  withdrew  to 
take  his  refection  of  bread  and  water,  and  then  returned 
again  to  the  chapels  till  after  midnight,  though  the 
weather  was  very  cold.  He  then  took  two  hours'  rest  on 
a  chair,  and  at  five  o'clock  in  the  morning  resumed  his 
devotions ;  then,  after  having  said  his  Mass,  he  again 
allowed  himself  a  small  portion  of  bread  and  water, 
and  continued  his  journey  to  Milan,  renewed  in  fervour 
of  spirit  and  with  a  firm  determination  to  begin  again 
to  serve  God  with  greater  energy  than  ever. 


48         Life  of  St.  Charles  Borromeo. 


This  same  year  God  was  pleased  to  permit  that  his 
Catholic  Majesty,  Philip  IL,  should  be  tried,  to  prove 
his  patience,  with  many  sorrows.  Besides  the  troubles 
in  his  Flemish  provinces,  within  three  months  he 
sustained  four  severe  losses  both  in  his  public  and 
private  relations.  The  first  was  the  death  of  his 
nephew  Sebastian,  King  of  Portugal,  who  having  gone 
with  his  army  against  the  Mahomedans  in  Africa,  fell 
in  a  disastrous  defeat  in  which  all  the  leaders  and 
most  of  his  troops  were  either  cut  to  pieces"  or  taken 
prisoners,  among  whom  were  the  Bishops  of  Coimbra 
and  Oporto,  the  flower  of  his  nobility,  and  a  great 
number  of  persons  of  consideration  of  different  nations. 
The  King  of  Spain  in  particular,  lost  many  valiant 
soldiers  whom  he  had  sent  to  attend  King  Sebastian. 
Soon  after  this,  he  lost  another  nephew,  Wenceslaus  of 
Austria,  his  sister's  son,  and  brother  of  the  Emperor 
Rudolph,  a  youth  of  great  promise  to  whom  he  was 
much  attached,  and  whom  he  always  kept  near  him 
at  his  court  About  the  same  time  died  in  the  prime 
of  life,  his  brother,  Don  John  of  Austria,  who  after 
his  victory  of  Lepanto,  had  been  entrusted  with  the 
government  of  Flanders,  where  he  died  waging  war 
with  the  rebels.  Death  also  deprived  him  of  his  son 
Ferdinand,  who  had  been  recognised  as  his  successor  on 
the  throne,  and  had  given  ground  for  hope  that  he  would 
inherit  his  father's  good  qualities. 

These  poignant  sorrows,  though  they  followed  one 
another  so  rapidly,  and  though  they  struck  so  closely 
home,  cutting  off  his  fairest  earthly  hopes,  did  not 
deprive  his  soul  of  its  constancy  and  conformity  to  the

will  of  God.  He  accepted  the  blows  at  His  hand 
with  resignation  like  Job,  turning  to  Him  in  a  child- 
like spirit,  and  praying  Him  not  to  abandon  him  in 
his  tribulations,  but  to  change  them  into  blessings  both 
for  himself  and  his  subjects. 

He  wrote  to  the  lieutenants  of  his  different  states, 
informing  them  of  his  affliction,  and  begging  them  to 
root  out  sin  and  everything  displeasing  to  God  from 
their  provinces,  and  to  join  with  their  people  in  prayer 
to  appease  His  anger  and  to  obtain  mercy  for  His 
Church. 

The  Governor  of  Milan  sent  this  letter  of  the  King 
to  St.  Charles,  that  he  might  co-operate  with  him  in 
carrying  out  his  wishes.  The  Saint  was  greatly  con- 
soled by  the  King's  Christian  spirit,  since  it  was  mani- 
fest that  however  sharply  he  had  been  wounded  by 
his  bereavements,  he  felt  dishonour  done  to  God  more 
deeply  still,  and  strove  earnestly  to  drive  out  sin  from 
among  his  people.  He  thought  the  letter  would  move 
the  Milanese  to  renewed  fervour,  and  therefore  had  it 
translated  and  published,  together  with  a  pastoral 
letter  from  himself.    It  ran  as  follows : — 

Letter  of  Philip  IL,  King  of  Spain,  to  the  Governor 
of  Milan.

self on  the  1 8th  of  this  present  October,  Ferdinand 
our  firstborn  son,  to  our  great  affliction  both  on 
account  of  his  virtues  and  being  heir  to  our  kingdom ; 
we  have  thought  it  well  to  inform  you  of  this  our  loss,

and  to  assure  you  that  bitter  as  it  is,  we  have 
received  it  as  coming  from  the  hand  of  God,  with 
entire  conformity  to  His  most  holy  will,  rendering

We  beg  you  also  in  a  Christian  spirit,  not  to  make  in

St.  Charles  entered  deeply  into  the  Bong's  senti- 
ments, sharing  alike  his  grief  for  the  losses  he  had 
sustained  and  his  desire  to  improve  them  in  the  way 
he  had  set  forth.  He  wrote  both  to  him  and  to  the 
Queen,  to  express  his  sympathy,  and  published  a 
pastoral,  dated  December  13,  1578,  calling  upon  the 
people  to  join  in  fervent  prayer  to  Almighty  God  for 
the  intentions  of  his  majesty. 

He  instituted  prayers  throughout  the  city,  beginning 
with  the  Forty  Hours'  Exposition  of  the  Blessed  Sacra- 
ment at  the  cathedral,  carrying  it  on  at  all  the  other 
churches,  and  had  processions  in  the  different  parishes,

and  an  hour's  prayer  offered  in  all  collegiate  and 
parochial  churches  on  festival  days  after  Vespers, 
and  ordered  the  Collect  for  the  King  to  be  said  at 
every  Mass.  To  this  he  added  exhortations  to  them 
to  join  in  more  abundant  almsgiving  and  to  increase 
their  fasts,  striving  by  every  means  in  their  power 
to  appease  the  anger  of  God  and  to  move  Him  to 
spare  their  sovereign  and  his  children,  to  bestow  upon 
them  every  blessing,  spiritual  and  temporal,  to  supply 
all  the  needs  of  the  Church,  and  to  have  mercy  on  the 
souls  of  the  deceased  princes. 

The  readiness  with  which  the  clergy  and  people 
responded  to  these  appeals  testified  to  their  loyalty 
and  affection  for  their  king ;  and  the  evidence  of  the 
sincerity  of  the  Saint's  sympathy  is  found  in  the 
earnestness  with  which  he  called  upon  all  to  join 
in  these  intercessions  and  added  to  his  own  penances 
and  prayers.

CHAPTER  VII. 

CONTINUED  OPPOSITION  OF  THE  GOVERNOR — PUBLICATION 
OF  THE  "  MEMORIALE." 

1579- 

We  have  al  ready  spoken  of  various  ways  in  which  the 
new  Governor  lent  himself  to  the  designs  of  the  per- 
verse faction  by  reviving  the  vexed  question  of  eccle- 
siastical jurisdiction,  and  not  shrinking  even  from  un- 
worthy means  in  order  to  injure  the  saint's  credit  and 
procure  a  decision  against  him  at  Rome.  We  have  seen 
how  unfounded  were  their  aspersions  upon  his  loyalty  to 
the  crown  of  Spain,  so  that  the  whole  was  clearly  the 
work  of  the  father  of  lies. 

There  was  worse,  however,  to  come.  The  Governor 
opened  up  again  the  whole  dispute  in  the  matter  of 
jurisdiction,  and  this  in  the  face  of  the  proof  the  King 
had  so  lately  given  of  his  favour  and  the  opinion  of  the 
Marquis  of  Alcanisio,1  a  gentleman  of  irreproachable 
character,  who,  having  lately  returned  to  Milan  from  a 
mission  to  Eome,  declared  without  reserve  that  the 
King  had  the  highest  veneration  for  the  Cardinal,  and 
that  it  was  ludicrous  to  suspect  him  of  harbouring 
any  disloyal  designs.    The  Governor  seems  to  have

them  of  the  mercies  of  God  in  their  deliverance  from 
the  plague,  and  of  the  ingratitude  of  provoking  His 
anger  by  the  commission  of  new  follies  and  sins.

"  "What  was  this  indeed,"  he  said,  "  but  to  call  down

This  pastoral  was  no  less  fruitful  than  usual,  but 
at  the  same  time  it  failed  to  win  the  compliance  of 
the  Governor  and  those  for  whom  it  was  especially 
designed.  They  seemed  rather  to  have  hardened  their 
hearts  more  obdurately  against  his  paternal  reproofs. 
Going  on  from  bad  to  worse,  they  were  promoting 
the  desecration  of  the  first  Sunday  of  Lent  by  masques, 
public  balls,  and  tournaments  in  direct  contravention 
of  the  Cardinal's  decree  in  his  provincial  council, 
already  accepted  by  the  people  as  a  precept  of  obliga- 
tion, which  could  not,  therefore,  be  transgressed  with- 
out giving  grave  scandal  and  committing  mortal  sin. 
When  St.  Charles  had  satisfied  himself  that  this  was 
no  vain  threat,  but  that  preparations  were  already 
made  for  giving  effect  to  it,  he  perceived  the  time 
was  come  to  exert  the  strong  hand  of  authority. 
Eemembering  that  he  was  chief  pastor  of  the  flock, 
he  knew  that  when  he  saw  the  wolf  coming,  it 
behoved  him  not  to  flee  like  a  hireling,  but  to  stand

it  was  in  vain  that  the  Saint  sought  to  disabuse  him 
by  means  of  mutual  friends,  or  to  convince  him  that 
he  had  acted  according  to  the  obligations  of  his  pastoral 
office.  Far  from  yielding  to  these  representations,  he 
suffered  himself  to  be  led  entirely  by  ill-intentioned

persons,  including  some  religious  of  no  very  edifying

There  were  some  religious,  who  understood  little 
about  the  obligations  and  difficulties  of  the  episco-

themselves  to  censure  and  abuse  the  Cardinal's

even  from  the  pulpit.  One  preacher  was  especially 
notorious  for  these  animadversions.  When  it  was 
reported  to  St.  Charles,  he  would  take  no  steps  to 
close  his  mouth,  but  left  it  entirely  in  God's  hands, 
giving  the  same  answer  which  David  in  bis  humility 
gave  to  the  curses  of  Semei,  that  God  had  permitted 
it,  and  he  would  not  resist  Him.  Some  persons  of 
consideration,  however,  represented  to  him  that  he 
was  letting  the  matter  go  too  far  in  allowing  the 
preacher  such  license,  that  it  was  a  public  scandal, 
which  might  prove  injurious  to  many  souls.  Even 
then  the  Saint  opposed  him  with  nothing  but  his 
own  meekness  and  forbearance,  and  left  it  to  his 
superiors  to  admonish  him.  The  preacher  did  not, 
however,  yield  as  yet,  when  at  last  the  Inquisitor, 
Father  Angelo  of  Cremona,  full  of  zeal  for  God  s 
glory,  acknowledged  that  he  could  not  allow  him  to 
go  on  with  impunity,  and  represented  to  the  Cardinal 
that  the  mischief  that  might  accrue  was  one  of  Satan's 
devices  for  the  introduction  of  heresy,  by  weakening 
the  consideration  of  the  people  for  the  dignity  and 
authority  of  their  pastor.  Mgr.  Jerome  Federici.

CHAPTER  VIIL 

FOUNDATION  OF  THE  CONVENT  OF  CAPUCHIN  NUNS  OR 
POOR  CLARES  OF  SANTA  PRASSEDE. 

I  579. 

While  the  servant  of  God  was  harassed  by  these  trials, 
our  Lord  vouchsafed  to  favour  him  with  a  great  spiritual 
consolation  in  the  foundation,  about  this  time,  of  a 
convent  of  nuns  who  sought  after  great  perfection. 
These  sisters  embraced  the  rule  of  St  Clare,  which 
binds  them  to  observe  a  perpetual  Lent,  to  sleep  upon 
boards  covered  only  with  a  single  blanket,  to  rise  in 
the  middle  of  the  night  for  matins,  to  chastise  their 
bodies  with  disciplines,  not  to  see  or  speak  with 
secular  persons,  even  near  relations,  to  wear  an  ash- 
coloured  habit  of  coarse  cloth  next  to  their  skin,  to  go 
barefoot  like  the  Capuchin  friars,  to  observe  with  great 
exactness  the  three  vows  of  religion,  to  be  assiduous  day 
and  night  in  prayer,  and  in  the  exercise  of  all  Christian 
virtues.  A  rule  indeed  of  great  bodily  severity,  but 
full  of  spiritual  consolations  ! 

A  lady,  Martha  Piantanida  by  name,  had  gathered 
together  in  her  house,  five  years  before,  a  number  of 
maidens  who  desired  to  lead  a  spiritual  life,  under  the 


Foundation  of  Convent  of  Capuchin  Nuns.  59 


direction  of  the  Regular  Clerks  of  St  Paul.  Our  Lord 
inspired  them  now  with  a  resolution  to  devote  them- 
selves to  Him  in  a  stricter  way.  They  accordingly 
applied  to  the  Cardinal  to  place  them  under  the  con- 
ventual rule  of  St.  Clare. 

Nothing  pleased  him  better,  for  he  had  long  de- 
sired to  see  a  convent  of  these  religious  established 
in  Milan,  and  he  promised,  therefore,  to  satisfy  their 
wishes  without  delay.  Having  further  examined  them, 
and  found  them  steadfast  in  their  determination,  he 
gave  them  enclosure  in  the  house  they  then  occupied, 
having  had  it  arranged  for  the  purpose,  intending  ulti- 
mately to  build  them  a  church  and  convent,  according 
to  the  rules  laid  down  by  himself  in  his  book  of  "  In- 
structions on  Ecclesiastical  Buildings."  He  appointed 
a  certain  number  of  pious  persons  to  undertake  the 
supervision  of  the  building,  and  bought  a  site  well 
adapted  for  the  purpose,  affording  ample  space  for  all 
the  necessary  offices,  garden,  and  cloister,  and  sur- 
rounded with  a  wall  which  at  once  enclosed  the 
convent  and  protected  it  from  being  overlooked  by 
surrounding  houses.  He  contributed  largely  himself 
to  -this  foundation  in  its  beginning  abd  during  his  life  : 
it  is  now  completed,  and,  allowing  for  the  simplicity 
and  poverty  required  by  the  rule,  it  may  be  said  to  be 
one  of  the  most  commodious  convents  of  Milan.  As 
the  Saint  set  great  store  by  this  foundation,  and 
reckoned  it  among  his  most  important  works,  he 
opened  it  with  solemnity,  with  the  view  also  of  mak- 
ing the  institute  known  to  the  people,  that  they  might 
be  liberal  in  alms  for  the  daily  support  of  the  nuns, 


6o         Life  of  St.  Charles  Borromeo. 


since  they  could  not  hold  any  property  either  indi- 
vidually or  in  common.  After  mass  on  Low  Sunday, 
April  26,  1 579,  he  blessed  the  habits  of  the  nuns  and 
clothed  eighteen  of  them  in  the  presence  of  a  large 
concourse  of  both  regular  and  secular  clergy  and  lay 
people.  After  the  clothing  he  laid  a  large  cross  upon 
the  shoulders  of  each  and  a  crown  of  thorns  on  their 
heads,  after  the  example  of  Him  whom  they  bad  chosen 
for  their  spouse,  and  thus  they  went  in  procession  to 
their  new  convent.  St.  Charles  gave  them  the  rule  of 
perpetual  enclosure  under  the  guidance  of  four  nuns  of 
the  same  order  whom  he  had  summoned  from  rerugia. 
At  the  same  time  he  blessed  and  laid  the  first  stone  of  a 
new  chapel  for  their  use  under  the  invocation  of  Santa 
Prassede,  granting  a  plenary  indulgence  to  all  who 
assisted  in  virtue  of  a  brief  which  he  had  obtained 
from  Rome.  He  made  a  decree  that  this  convent 
should  always  remain  under  the  Archbishops  of  Milan. 
The  blessing  of  God  has  manifestly  rested  upon  this 
work,  which  has  gone  on  increasing  to  this  day,  now 
counting  more  than  fifty  nuns,  among  whom  are 
daughters  of  the  noblest  families  of  Milan,  who  have 
passed  from  a  life  of  ease  to  one  of  seemingly  intoler- 
able austerity.  But  though  their  rule  is  severe 
externally,  the  grace  of  God  compensates  abundantly 
for  all  their  mortifications,  that  they  not  only  bear 
them  cheerfully,  but  rejoice  in  them  in  the  joy  of  the 
Holy  Ghost.  So  edifying  has  been  their  mode  of  life 
that  they  have  always  been  looked  upon  as  examples 
of  perfection,  and  their  prayers  are  constantly  asked  by 
the  people  in  all  necessities  and  trials.    The  odour  of 


Foundation  of  Convent  of  Capuchin  Nuns.  6 1 


their  sanctity  has  spread  far  and  wide,  and  the  people 
of  Pavia  and  Cremona  have  applied  to  them  to  estab- 
lish convents  of  the  order  in  their  own  cities. 

While  we  are  upon  this  subject,  we  must  not  omit 
to  mention  the  signal  example  of  the  Countess  Corona,1 
daughter  of  the  Count  John  Baptist  Borromeo,  who, 
desirous  of  imitating  the  holy  life  of  the  Cardinal  her 
uncle,  entered  as  a  nun  into  this  convent,  treading 
beneath  her  feet  the  grandeurs  and  pleasures  of  this 
world.  Preferring  the  love  of  Christ  to  all  the  brilliant 
allurements  that  surrounded  her  path  in  the  world, 
she  gladly  put  on  the  rough  habit  and  girdle  of  rope, 
devoting  herself  with  a  pure  intention  to  the  life  of 
penance  in  the  convent  of  Santa  Prassede,  where  she 
took  the  name  of  Sister  Helen.  In  entering  it  she  had 
desired  to  taste  of  suffering  for  the  love  of  God,  and 
our  Lord  granted  her  wish  by  sending  her  the  heavy 
cross  of  a  life-long  illness,  accompanied  with  suffer- 
ings so  great  that  it  might  well  be  reckoned  a  martyr- 
dom, and  a  perfect  example  of  patience  and  con- 
formity with  the  will  of  God.  After  she  had  been 
thus  tried  and  refined  in  His  love  for  three  years  and 
three  months,  He  called  her  to  receive  the  reward  of 
glory  she  had  merited,  leaving  behind  her  a  great 
reputation  for  sanctity.  Among  her  virtues  none 
was  perhaps  more  remarkable  than  her  spirit  of  obe- 
dience, which  was  exemplified  even  after  her  death. 
Though  the  nuns  had  closed  her  eyes,  they  afterwards 
found  them  open  on  several  occasions,  until  the  Mother

Hippolyta,  wife  of  Count  Alberico  Belgiojoso.

Abbess,  Sister  Jeronima  of  Perugia,  placing  her  hand 
upon  them,  said,  "  My  daughter,  as  you  have  always 
been  most  obedient  during  life,  so  now  obey  me  and

CHAPTER  IX. 


FIFTII  PROVINCIAL  COUNCIL — TRANSLATION  OF  THE 


Although  the  decrees  of  the  Fourth  and  last  Pro- 
vincial Council  had  not  yet  received  the  formal  con- 
firmation of  the  Holy  See,  as  it  was  now  three  years 
since  its  close,  the  Cardinal  began  his  preparations 
for  holding  the  fifth.  He  desired,  in  particular,  to 
insert  in  its  Acts  the  measures  adopted  by  him  during 
the  late  visitation  of  the  plague,  as  a  guide  to  other 
prelates  and  pastors  in  similar  emergencies. 

He  had  learnt  by  experience  that  at  such  times, 
if  men  are  not  prepared  with  the  knowledge  how 
to  grapple  with  them,  they  are  apt  to  be  over- 
whelmed with  solicitude  and  deprived  by  their 
anxiety  of  the  power  of  forming  a  correct  judg- 
ment. A  concise  statement  of  all  his  regulations 
may  be  found  preserved  in  the  second  part  of  the 
Acts  of  this  Council,  which  was  held  early  in  May 
of  the  year  1579,  having  been  attended  by  the 
bishops  of  the  province  as  usual.  Many  other  use- 
ful decrees  were  also  published  concerning  the  defence

of  the  Catholic  faith,  the  reverence  due  to  holy  seasons
