canvas,  and  a  straw  pillow  completed  the  bed  on 
which  the  Saint  took  his  rest  during  the  remainder 
of  his  life.

When  the  church  had  been  restored,  the  saint  gave

CHAPTER  X.

The  labours  of  the  Provincial  Council  were  no  sooner 
brought  to  a  close  than  the  Saint  began  to  prepare  for 
the  next  Diocesan  Synod,  which  he  had  never  omitted, 
except  when  he  had  been  legitimately  prevented,  and 
then  he  had  always  asked  for  the  permission  of  the 
Supreme  Pontiff  to  transfer  it  to  another  season,  so  as 
not  to  break  through  the  order  of  the  Council  of 
Trent.  This  year  he  called  together  his  clergy  for  the 
1 2th  of  June,  when,  besides  fulfilling  the  appointed

in  the  hearts  of  his  priests,  impressing  this  upon  them 
particularly  in  three  discourses  full  of  the  Spirit  of 


At  its  close  he  gave  to  all  the  priests  who  desired 
it  the  usual  audiences,  and  was  asked  by  the  Jesuit 
Fathers  to  dedicate  their  new  Church  of  St.  Fidelis. 
Accordingly,  on  the  24th  of  June  he  went  thither  pro-

cessionally  with  the  Chapter  of  the  cathedral,  and

The  zeal  of  the  Saint  kept  him  ever  on  the  watch 
for  new  occasions  of  benefiting  his  people  and  procur- 
ing for  all  the  means  of  attaining  eternal  life.  At  this 
time  he  had  before  his  mind  particularly  the  case  of 
those  unhappy  women,  who,  in  giving  themselves  over 
to  a  life  of  sin,  not  only  lose  their  own  souls,  but  draw 
multitudes  of  others  to  perdition,  thus  infinitely  mul- 
tiplying the  dishonour  done  to  God.  He  found  two 
houses  already  established  in  the  city  for  their  relief : 
first,  a  convent  where  they  made  a  religious  profession 
with  the  three  solemn  vows  under  the  name  of  the 
"  Convent  of  the  Crucified ; "  secondly,  the  house  of 
St.  Valeria,  where  a  rule  without  vows  is  observed. 
He  fostered  and  encouraged  these  two  institutions  by 
his  alms  and  counsel;  but  they  did  not  suffice  to 
receive  all  who  presented  themselves,  nor  did  the 
House  of  Succour 1  he  had  founded  make  up  for  the 
deficiency.    He  determined  therefore  to  establish  a

new  house  capable  of  receiving  all  who  should  make 
application  with  the  recommendation  of  the  Arch-

Four  years  before  he  had  made  a  small  begin- 
ning by  hiring  a  house  for  the  purpose,  and  now

made  a  permanent  foundation  under  a  legal  instru-

its  affairs.  This  house  was  called  the  "  Depositor}'," 
and  he  placed  it  under  the  protection  of  St.  Mary 
Magdalen,  on  whose  festival  these  arrangements  were 
completed.  He  provided  it  with  a  confessor  in 
ordinary,  whose  charge  was  to  deliver  these  poor 
creatures  from  their  sin,  and  to  put  them  in  the  way 
of  salvation,  confiding  the  internal  government  to 
pious  women  of  sufficient  experience.  He  gave  it 
the  name  of  the  Depository,  to  signify  that  it  was 
intended  as  a  temporary  abode  from  which  the  in- 
mates might  either  enter  the  marriage  state,  or  devote 
themselves  in  the  Convent  of  the  Crucified,  or  among 
the  penitents  of  St.  Valeria,  or  adopt  any  respectable 
calling  in  the  world. 

This  good  work  was  never  lost  sight  of  by  St. 
Charles,  being  aided  by  his  alms  from  time  to  time, 
and  has  been  blessed  by  being  the  means  of  saving 
many  souls.

CHAPTER  XL 


CHAPTER  OP  THE  FATHERS  OP  CONGREGATION  OF  ST. 
PAUL,  AND  OF  THE  BROTHERS  OF  ST.  AMBROSE 
AD  NEMUS. 


Among  the  institutions  of  Milan  none  is  more  worthy 
of  mention  than  the  Venerable  Congregation  of  the 
Regular  Clerks  of  St.  Paul,  commonly  called  Barna- 
bites.  It  was  founded  in  this  city  about  the  year 
1530  by  three  priests,  viz.,  Antonio  Maria  Zaccaria 
of  Cremona,  and  Bartholomew  Ferrari  and  James 
Antony  Morigia,  both  of  Milan.  All  three  belonged 
to  noble  families,  but  withdrew  from  the  world  to 
devote  themselves  to  the  service  of  God  in  a  life  of 
perfection,  and  to  labour  for  the  salvation  of  souls. 
They  were  soon  joined  by  others  who  shared  their 
zeal  and  devotion,  and  were  ultimately  formed  into 
a  Congregation  under  the  authority  of  the  Holy  See. 
They  received  the  name  of  Barnabites  from  the 
church  dedicated  to  St.  Barnabas,  which  they  served 
in  Milan.  Under  the  blessing  of  God  their  Congrega- 
tion increased  both  in  numbers  and  in  the  fruits  of 
their  labours,  and  soon  spread  to  other  cities  of  Italy. 
Their  work  was  to  hear  confessions,  to  preach  to  the

people,  and  to  hold  themselves  at  the  disposition  of 
the  Bishops  in  their  pastoral  labours. 

This  Congregation  has  produced  many  excellent 
priests;  among  them  two  particularly  eminent  for 
piety.  First,  Father  Alexander  Sauli  of  Genoa, 
Bishop,  first  of  Aleria,  in  Corsica,  afterwards  of 
Pavia.  Of  his  virtues  I  can  speak  with  confidence, 
as  they  were  intimately  known  to  me  through  a 
long  course  of  years,  and  won  him  the  sincere 
esteem  and  attachment  of  St.  Charles.  When  he 
passed  to  a  better  life,  so  great  was  the  reputation 
of  his  sanctity  that  the  people  ran  in  crowds  to 
touch  his  bier  with  their  rosaries.  His  tomb  in  the 
cathedral  church  of  Pavia  has  never  ceased  to  be 
visited  by  numbers  of  clients  anxious  to  obtain  his 
intercession,  the  fruit  of  which  is  testified  by  ex 
votos  placed  in  grateful  remembrance. 

The  other  was  Father  Charles  Bascapfe,  of  a  noble 
Milanese  family,  whose  name  has  already  been  men- 
tioned, and  will  frequently  appear  in  the  course  of 
this  history.  When  in  the  College  of  Advocates  in 
Milan,  St  Charles  recognised  his  talents,  and  made 
him  Canon  in  Ordinary  of  the  cathedral,  employing 
him  in  various  way  in  his  diocese.  Believing  him- 
self to  be  called  by  God  to  a  more  perfect  life,  he 
entered  the  Congregation  of  St  Paul,  in  which  he  soon 
rose  to  the  highest  offices.1  It  is  to  his  labours  that 
we  owe  the  history  of  the  life  of  our  Saint  in  Latin, 
which  we  have  endeavoured  to  reproduce  in  these 
pages  in  the  vulgar  tongue.

When  this  Congregation  had  increased  in  numbers 
and  importance,  their  original  constitutions,  which  were 
very  brief,  required  to  be  revised.  In  order  that  all 
might  be  done  with  exactness,  the  permission  of  the 
Holy  See  was  obtained  that  St.  Charles  should  preside 
over  their  deliberations.  Under  his  auspices  the  work 
was  brought  to  a  conclusion,  and  afterwards  received 
the  approbation  of  Gregory  XIII.  in  a  special  Bull. 
Great  harmony  and  mutual  esteem  had  reigned  from 
the  first  between  these  fathers  and  their  Archbishop, 
and  this  issue  of  their  labours  gave  him  great  joy.  He 
always  warmly  acknowledged  their  merits,  employing 
them  in  the  various  offices  of  the  diocese,  living  in 
great  intimacy  with  them,  and  often  withdrew  for  a 
time  from  his  public  duties  for  spiritual  retirement  at 
St.  Barnabas,  and  other  houses  of  their  Congregation ; 
while  they,  on  their  part,  were  always  most  devoted  to 
him,  and  ready  to  lend  themselves  to  all  his  wishes. 

Soon  after  this  he  was  asked  to  perform  the  same 
office  for  the  brothers  of  St.  Ambrose  ad  nemiis,  whose 
monastery  is  situated  in  the  environs  of  Milan.  They 
were  about  to  hold  a  General  Chapter,  and  applied  for 
the  permission  of  the  Apostolic  See  to  that  effect. 
With  his  assistance  rules  were  made  for  the  govern- 
ment of  the  institute,  which  had  been  founded  by 
three  Milanese  of  good  families,  viz.,  Alexander  Cri- 
vello,  Albert  Besozzo,  and  Antonio  Pietra  Santa,  who 
had  devoted  themselves  to  a  life  of  seclusion  in  the 
midst  of  a  wood,  whence  the  church  still  retains  the 
name  of  St  Ambrose  ad  nemus,  or  u  in  the  wood."  It 
was  dedicated  to  St.  Ambrose  in  the  first  instance

because  that  saint  used  to  frequent  the  spot  for  con- 
templation and  retirement  The  fame  of  these  first 
recluses  drew  numbers  to  follow  them,  and  in  process 
of  time  they  grew  under  Apostolic  sanction  into  a 
Regular  Congregation,  using  the  Ambrosian  Rite  with

cost  when  it  was  a  question  of  promoting  what  he  had 
most  at  heart,  viz.,  the  revival  in  religious  communi- 
ties of  discipline  and  ancient  observance.

CHAPTER  XIL 


VISITATION*  OF  THE  DIOCESES  OF  VIGEVANO  AND  OF  COMO 

 AN  APOSTOLIC  NUNCIO  SENT  TO  SWITZERLAND  

FOUNDATION  OF  THE  SWISS  COLLEGE. 


As  the  entire  cessation  of  the  plague  now  gave  him 
some  little  liberty,  St  Charles  resolved  to  continue 
the  visitation  of  the  province,  which  he  had  begun  at 
Cremona  and  Bergamo,  taking  Vigevano  next  in  order, 
which,  being  a  small  diocese,  would  not  require  him  to 
be  long  absent  from  his  own  see.  Having  given  notice 
of  his  intention,  the  citizens  of  Vigevano  prepared 
to  receive  him  with  every  mark  of  honour.  Setting 
to  work  with  his  accustomed  energy,  he  gained  in 
a  few  days  a  good  knowledge  of  the  needs  of  the  dio- 
cese ;  nor  did  he  return  without  having  endeavoured, 
by  preaching  daily  to  the  people,  to  quicken  them  in 
the  fear  and  love  of  God,  and  giving  them  an  oppor- 
tunity of  approaching  the  Sacraments.  He  provided 
also  for  the  worthier  celebration  of  the  Divine  offices 
in  the  churches,  and  by  these  and  other  blessings  con- 
ferred upon  them,  so  endeared  himself  to  all  the 
people  that  they  have  always  held  his  memory  in

Visits  Dioceses  of  Vigevano  and  Como.  75 


veneration.  Neither  has  this  feeling  passed  away  with 
time,  for  we  have  lately  seen  the  people  of  this  city 
come  in  solemn  procession  to  visit  the  Saint's  tomb, 
accompanied  with  trumpets  and  choirs  of  musicians. 
Among  the  offerings  which  they  brought  with  them 
was  a  banner  on  which  was  represented,  in  em-

From  Vigevano  he  went  on  to  visit  some  parts  of 
his  own  diocese,  where  great  havoc  had  been  made 
among  the  flock  by  disobedience  to  the  decrees  of  his 
synods.  The  opposition  shown  by  the  Governor  to 
his  measures  of  reform,  and  the  encouragement  given 
by  him  to  licentious  amusements,  had  not  escaped 
notice,  and  afforded  a  pretext  to  dissolute  persons  to 
give  themselves  up  to  such  pastimes.  Nor  had  they 
any  respect  to  the  commands  of  their  Archbishop, 
since  they  reckoned  that  the  example  of  their  betters 
was  sufficient  excuse  for  themselves  to  set  them  at 
nought.  In  this  way  the  old  scandals  and  abuses  of 
public  balls  and  other  profanities,  on  Sundays  and 
holidays,  had  again  crept  into  many  places.  To  such 
a  pass  had  this  spirit  gone  that  during  the  Cardinals 
visitation — a  time  when  it  was  customary  for  all  to 
put  business  and  pleasure  aside,  and  frequent  the 
Sacraments — certain  persons  dared  to  hold  great  public 
festival  on  a  holy  day  of  the  Church,  using  force  and 
violence  to  those  who  wished  to  avail  themselves  of 
the  means  of  grace,  in  order  to  prevail  upon  them  to 
join  them.  Distressed  as  he  was  at  this  scandal,  he 
would  not  at  first  visit  it  with  the  penalties  he  might

76 


Life  of  St.  Charles  Borromeo. 


have  used,  knowing  that  the  mischief  took  its  origin 
from  a  higher  source,  and  he  hoped  by  patient  endur- 
ance to  restore  order  by  pacific  measures. 

When  men  in  high  places  set  the  example  of 
contempt  for  their  spiritual  rulers  and  the  laws  of 
the  Church,  it  cannot  be  expected  that  the  common 
people  should  not  indulge  in  similar  excesses.  This 
is  one  way  in  which  God  chastises  the  sins  of  princes 
by  making  them  react  upon  themselves.  The  license 
which  they  have  themselves  taught  the  people  in 
reference  to  moral  and  ecclesiastical  precepts  soon 
accustoms  the  latter  to  the  disregard  of  civil  laws  also, 
and  thus  are  sown  seeds  of  revolt  which  ultimately 
bear  their  fruit  in  outbreaks  of  the  populace  and  over- 
throw of  governments.  The  secular  arm  will  not  long 
continue  to  be  obeyed  where  respect  has  ceased  for 
that  spiritual  authority  which  is  the  reign  of  God 
Himself  upon  earth. 

In  the  meantime  it  became  clear  to  St  Charles  that 
it  would  not  be  possible  to  make  himself  personally 
acquainted  with  the  whole  province,  and  that  it  was 
undesirable  to  absent  himself  any  longer  from  the 
capital.  With  the  consent  of  the  Pontiff,  therefore, 
other  visitors  were  appointed  to  finish  the  work,  Brescia 
only  being  reserved  for  his  own  supervision  besides 
those  he  had  already  visited. 

In  pursuance  of  this  arrangement,  His  Holiness 
appointed  the  Bishop  of  Famagosta  to  undertake  the 
rest  of  the  work,  after  finishing  the  visitation  of  Milan 
itself.  Mgr.  Francesco  Bosso,  Bishop  of  Novara,  was 
to  take  Lodi  in  charge,  and  Mgr.  Giovanni  Francesco

Bonomo,  Bishop  of  Vercelli,  to  undertake  the  visitation 
of  No  vara.  At  the  request  of  St  Charles,  however, 
these  dispositions  were  subsequently  altered  so  far 
that  Mgr.  Bonomo  was  appointed  for  the  visitation  of 
Como  instead  of  Novara,  because  Como  afforded  full 
scope  for  the  exercise  of  his  zeal,  both  on  account  of 
its  size,  and  because  it  extended  some  distance  into  the 
territory  of  Switzerland  and  the  Grisons,  from  which 
parts  heresy  had  spread  into  the  valleys  of  Chiavenna 
and  Valtellina,  while  the  Bishop  of  Como,  being  aged 
and  infirm,  was  unable  to  grapple  with  the  increasing 
evil.  Although  Como  did  not  belong  to  the  ecclesias- 
tical province  under  the  saint's  jurisdiction,  yet  its 
nearness  was  sufficient  to  establish  a  claim  upon  his 
charity.  The  Bishop  of  Vercelli,  knowing  his  prudence, 
would  not  set  out  on  this  mission  without  first  resorting 
to  him  for  advice  on  the  difficult  matter  of  treating 
with  the  people  of  Switzerland  and  the  Grisons. 

St  Charles  had  before  this  brought  about  the 
establishment  of  a  Nuncio  Apostolic  to  these  parts 
for  the  promotion  of  the  Catholic  faith,  a  mission 
which  was  greatly  needed,  for  ecclesiastical  affairs  in 
those  states  were  at  this  time  by  no  means  flourishing. 
Finding  that  the  Bishop  of  Vercelli  had  conducted  the 
visitation  of  Como  with  great  prudence,  the  Saint  pro- 
posed him  to  the  Holy  See  as  a  fit  person  for  this 
Nunciature.  Gregory  XIII.  immediately  made  the 
desired  appointment,  and  gave  him  as  his  Auditor, 
Marcantonio  Bellini,  who  was  afterwards  Canon  in 
Ordinary  and  Chancellor  of  Milan,  and  at  the  present 
moment  Bishop  of  Bobbio.

The  Bishop  of  Novara  filled  the  office  of  Nuncio  for 
two  years,  during  which  time,  aided  by  the  counsels 
of  St  Charles,  he  did  good  service  to  the  Church  in 
reforming  the  clergy,  introducing  the  observance  of  the 
decrees  of  the  Council  of  Trent,  and  effecting  many 
other  improvements,  to  the  great  satisfaction  of  His 
Holiness,  who  next  employed  him  as  Nuncio  to  the 
Emperor  in  the  year  1581,  and  intrusted  to  him  the 
delicate  commission  of  deposing  Gebhard  Truchses, 
Archbishop  of  Cologne,  together  with  the  Provost  and 
some  of  the  Canons  who  sided  with  the  Bishop,  and  of 
assembling  the  Chapter  for  the  election  of  a  new  pre- 
late. In  this  business  he  also  succeeded,  and  under 
his  auspices  the  suffrages  were  given  in  favour  of  a 
good  Catholic  prelate,  Ernest,  son  of  the  Duke  of 
Bavaria.  Another  work  which  he  found  means  to 
accomplish,  was  to  send  the  notorious  heretic,  James 
Palaeologus,  for  trial  at  Rome.  When  he  had  been 
about  three  years  at  this  post,  he  was  sent  by  the 
Pope,  with  the  title  of  Apostolic  Nuncio,  into  the  Low 
Countries,  which  at  that  time  stood  in  great  need  of 
such  assistance,  on  account  of  the  heresies  which  had 
made  havoc  there.  He  laboured  there  for  two  years, 
and  was  called  away  in  the  midst  of  his  toils  at  liege 
on  the  26th  February  1587.  He  left  all  his  property 
at  his  death  to  the  Monte  di  Pieti,  founded  by  himself 
at  Yercelli,  in  order  to  imitate  his  master  St.  Charles, 
whose  memory  he  has  celebrated  in  some  Latin  verses 
on  the  wonderful  preservation  of  the  Saint,  by  whom 
he  had  been  consecrated  Bishop,  and  who  renounced 
in  his  favour  the  abbacy  of  Nonantula.    Since  this

time  the  Holy  See  has  always  continued  to  send  a 
Nuncio  to  Switzerland,  who  has  been  received  with 
every  mark  of  honour. 

St  Charles'  exertions  in  behalf  of  Swiss  Catholics 
did  not  end  here.  He  this  year  laid  the  founda- 
tion of  a  college  for  Swiss  priests  in  Milan,  a  work 
which  had  long  occupied  his  thoughts,  and  formed  a 
subject  of  consultation  with  the  Holy  Father.  He 
well  knew  that  there  was  no  means  of  promoting  the 
Catholic  faith  so  effectual  as  the  provision  of  priests 
sufficiently  well  instructed  to  teach  the  mysteries  of 
religion,  who  should  by  their  life  and  conduct  elevate 
and  edify  their  flock.  Of  such  there  was  great 
lack,  and  total  absence,  moreover,  of  the  means  of 
supplying  the  deficiency.  This  he  felt  most  urgently 
with  respect  to  the  territory  of  the  Grisons,  where 
Satan  had  contrived  almost  entirely  to  obscure  the 
light  of  truth.  The  civil  authorities  had  prohibited 
any  but  Swiss  ecclesiastics  from  entering  the  country, 
and  as  heretical  opinions  reigned  at  Coira,  where  the 
only  seminary  was,  no  fresh  priests  could  be  ordained. 
In  this  way  the  authorities  reckoned  they  should  in  a 
short  time  cut  off  religion  at  its  source.  Meantime 
the  people,  being  deprived  of  pastors,  were  driven  to 
attend  the  preachings  of  false  teachers,  from  whom 
they  imbibed  pestilent  doctrine,  which  they  had  not 
the  wit  to  gainsay,  and  thus  their  souls  day  by  day 
fell  a  prey  to  the  enemy.  The  scheme  was  undeniably 
well  devised,  and  might  have  ended  in  total  loss  of 
faith,  had  not  God  in  His  mercy  raised  up  St.  Charles 
and  enabled  him  to  repair  the  mischief.

Such  was  the  origin  of  the  Swiss  or  Helvetian 
College  founded  by  the  Saint  in  thi3  year,  1579.  In 
drawing  up  its  rules  he  received  every  faculty  and 
privilege  from  the  Holy  See.  In  the  first  instance 
he  made  the  full  number  of  students  to  be  forty,  of 
whom  half  were  to  be  Swiss,  and  half  natives  of  the 
Grisons,  the  perpetual  administration  of  the  college 
being  reserved  to  the  Archbishop  of  Milan  for  the 
time  being.  The  internal  direction  he  gave  to  the 
Oblates  of  St.  Ambrose,  with  rules  like  those  of  his 
own  seminar}',  the  students  attending  the  schools  of 
the  Jesuit  Fathers  in  the  College  of  Brera,  founded 
also  by  himself.  He  obtained  for  them  from  Cardinal 
Alessandrino  the  house  and  church  of  the  Holy  Spirit, 
which  had  formerly  belonged  to  the  Umiliati.  He 
subsequently  removed  it  to  a  more  salubrious  situation 
in  a  convent,  the  nuns  of  which  he,  by  Apostolic  autho- 
rity, transferred  and  united  to  the  sisters  of  Santa  Maria 
al  Cerchio. 

In  this  foundation,  the  Supreme  Pontiff  and  many  of 
the  Cardinals  helped  him  liberally  with  alms.  He  after- 
wards assigned  to  it  the  revenues  of  two  benefices  which 
fell  in  to  him,  one  at  Monza,  the  other  at  Novara,  and 
not  long  afterwards  the  benefice  of  St.  Anthony  at  Pa  via 
also.  Within  a  year  and  a  half  he  procured  from  his 
cousin  Cardinal  Altaemps,  Bishop  of  Constance,  a  grant 
duly  secured  under  an  Apostolic  Bull  of  the  benefice 
of  Mirasole  near  Milan,  with  the  stipulation  that  four- 
and-twenty  youths  of  the  diocese  of  Constance  should 
be  maintained  in  the  college  during  his  life,  and  four- 
teen during  the  lives  of  his  two  immediate  successors.

By  these  means  he  provided  the  college  with  a  fixed 
income  of  eight  hundred  crowns.  A  commission  of  six 
ecclesiastics  was  appointed  by  him  for  the  administra- 
tion of  these  revenues*  It  was  his  good  pleasure  that 
I,  John  Peter  Giussano,  the  writer  of  this  work,  should 
be  of  this  number,  and  this  office  made  me  well  ac- 
quainted with  the  affection  he  bore  the  students  and 
his  solicitude  for  them  as  future  propagators  and  de- 
fenders of  the  faith.  He  obtained  from  the  Holy  See 
several  privileges  to  be  exercised  by  the  Archbishops 
of  Milan  in  its  favour ;  such  as  permission  to  ordain 
its  members  after  three  years  of  study,  for  which  pur- 
pose he  created  certain  titles  annexed  to  the  chapel  of 
the  college,  upon  which  he  could  ordain  them  as  if  he 
were  their  diocesan,  also  a  faculty  to  confer  the  degree 
of  Doctor  of  Theology  on  those  who  had  finished  their 
course  of  philosophy  and  theology,  so  that  being  duly 
invested  with  the  character  of  priests  and  the  degree 
of  doctor  there  should  be  no  further  impediment  in 
the  way  of  their  at  once  going  out  to  work  in  the 
vineyard  in  obedience  to  their  several  bishops,  for 
before  admission  to  the  college  they  were  required  to 
take  an  oath  that  at  the  close  of  their  studies  they 
would  devote  themselves  to  labour  in  their  own  country 
— the  object  for  which  the  college  was  founded.  He 
obtained  also  certain  indulgences  for  such  of  its  mem- 
bers as  should  be  enrolled  in  a  confraternity  of  the 
Blessed  Virgin  attached  to  the  college. 

This  pious  work  of  our  saint  has  abundantly  answered 
his  intentions,  and  continually  supplies  Switzerland  and 
the  Grisons  with  pastors  sound  in  doctrine  and  blameless

in  life,  by  whose  labours  heresy  has  been  quelled  and 
discipline  restored.  We  shall  have  occasion  to  speak

CHAPTER  I. 


ECCLESIASTICAL  AFFAIRS  AT  ROME  VISITS  TO  HOLY 


When  the  Governor  of  Milan,  who  was  already  pre- 
judiced against  our  Saint,  saw  his  favourite  preacher 
removed  in  the  middle  of  his  Lenten  course  of  sermons, 
as  he  had  himself  requested  the  General  of  his  order 
to  allow  him  to  preach,  he  felt  much  annoyed,  think- 
ing that  the  Cardinal  had  done  it  on  purpose  to  flout 
him.  As  usual,  there  were  not  wanting  evil  counsellors 
to  confirm  him  in  this  opinion  and  to  urge  him  to  show 
his  resentment.  Besides  the  efforts  made  by  some  of 
the  fathers  of  the  order  to  prove  to  the  world  that 
the  Cardinal  was  in  the  wrong,  the  Governor  himself 
had  written  to  Eome  complaining  bitterly  of  the  way 
in  which  he  had  been  treated,  and  begging  them  to 
hasten  their  decision,  and  to  take  into  consideration 
some  other  charges  formerly  brought  against  the  Saint 
He  used  all  his  influence  at  the  Soman  Court  by

partisans  and  others  to  spread  injurious  reports  and  to

As  the  decrees  of  the  Fourth  Provincial  Council  of 
Milan  were  awaiting  confirmation  at  that  time,  there 
were  not  wanting  some  who  openly  found  fault  with 
them,  and  strove  in  every  way  to  lessen  their  authority, 
saying  that  so  much  liberty  ought  not  to  be  allowed 
to  the  Cardinal.  The  spiritual  edifice,  that  the  watch- 
fulness of  the  servant  of  God  had  raised  up  in  so  many 
years,  was  thus  imperilled  by  the  malice  of  Satan. 
Besides  the  evil  reports  spread  in  Rome,  additional 
efforts  were  made  to  defame  him  in  Milan.  It  was 
repeated  that  he  was  a  man  void  of  prudence,  that  he 
was  disliked  by  many,  that  the  King  of  Spain  had 
desired  his  ambassador  to  have  him  removed,  and  had 
directed  the  Governor  to  proceed  against  him  with 
strong  measures.  Other  like  rumours  were  indus- 
triously spread  abroad  by  his  enemies,  in  the  hope 
that,  on  his  going  to  Eome,  he  would  not  be  allowed 
to  return.  These  lies  had  a  bad  effect  upon  men  of 
the  world,  who,  as  if  freed  from  all  restraint,  thought 
themselves  at  liberty  to  do  as  they  liked  without  any 
regard  to  the  laws  of  the  Church. 

Mgr.  Speciano,  in  reporting  this  state  of  affairs  from 
Eome,  wrote  that  he  was  no  longer  able  to  obtain 
audiences  as  formerly;  that  he  thought  it  expedient 
that  the  Cardinal  should  come  in  person  and  defend 
his  cause  before  he  should  be  attacked  with  greater 
violence.  The  good  pastor  thereupon  perceived  that 
he  was  in  a  difficult  position,  and  although  he  had 
never  hitherto  gone  to  Eome  on  account  of  intrigues

against  himself,  and  had  left  such  matters  to  the

As  he  was  visiting  the  district  of  Desio  at  this  time,

season.  While  preparing  to  start  after  the  feast  of

Domenico  Bollano,  the  Bishop  of  Brescia,  was  dying. 
Upon  which  he  instantly  started  for  that  city  and 
arrived  in  time  to  administer  the  last  sacraments,

thousand  persons. 

From  thence  he  went  to  Mantua  to  consult  with 
his  widowed  sister  Camilla,  on  family  affairs,  and  was 
received  with  great  kindness  by  the  Duke  of  Mantua. 
On  leaving  by  way  of  Bologna  for  Rome,  he  was  asked 
by  his  attendants  where  he  meant  to  stop  on  the

u  Where  the  Lord  wills,"  he  replied,  giving  them  to 
understand  that  he  wished  no  preparations  to  be  made 
for  him,  but  was  content  to  put  up  with  any  incon-

As  he  was  well  aware  that  the  storm  which  was

to  retire  for  a  while  to  the  hermitage  of  Camaldoli,  in 
order  to  treat  with  our  Lord  alone  on  the  matter. 
This  retreat  is  situated  in  the  Apennines,  between 
Tuscany  and  the  Eomagna,  in  a  wild  district  where 
the  roads  were  bad.  While  he  was  riding  thither 
through  the  mountains,  he  was  overtaken  by  night 
in  a  part  unknown  to  him ;  and  as  he  was  passing  a 
little  church  dedicated  to  St.  Michael,  the  priest  living 
there  heard  the  tramp  of  horses'  feet,  and  going  out, 
cried,  "Stop,  stop!"  At  this  the  Cardinal  stopped, 
and  the  priest  coming  up,  asked  where  he  was  going. 
On  his  replying  to  Camaldoli,  the  priest  said  he  could 
go  no  further  that  night,  but  must  stay  with  him,  as 
the  roads  were  dangerous,  and  not  safe  even  in  the 
day-time.  The  Saint  took  his  advice,  and  remained 
with  him,  though  there  was  but  small  provision  for 
supper,  and  only  one  poor  bed  to  lie  on.  After  eating 
a  little  food  he  withdrew  to  the  church,  where  he 
remained  all  night  in  prayer,  allowing  his  attendants 
to  take  it  in  turns  to  pray  with  him,  while  the  rest 
slept  upon  straw,  in  order  not  to  deprive  the  poor 
priest  of  his  bed.    The  next  morning  he  proceeded

on  his  way,  and  had  scarcely  gone  half  a  mile  when,

.  Owing  to  his  long  retreat,  the  report  was  spread 
that  he  had  abandoned  the  world  and  had  become  a

by  well-disposed  persons. 

From  Camaldoli  he  went  to  Mount  Alvernia,  where 
the  glorious  St.  Francis  received  the  stigmata  from  our 
Lord,  giving  himself  there  up  to  the  contemplation  of 
heavenly  things,  and  meditation  on  the  seraphic  spirit 
of  St  Francis,  and  the  flame  of  love  that  burnt  in  his 
heart  In  this  retreat  he  not  only  gained  new  fervour, 
but  likewise  a  strong  desire  to  suffer  every  kind  of 
opposition  for  the  love  of  God.  Eenewed  in  spirit, 
he  then  went  on  to  the  holy  house  of  Loreto,  being 
warmly  received  by  Francis  Mary,  Duke  of  Urbino, 
as  he  passed  through  his  territory.  Out  of  devotion 
he  went  on  foot  from  Fossombrone  to  Loreto,  a  dis-

tance  of  not  less  than  fifty  miles,  with  his  spirit  intent 
upon  God,  meditating,  praying,  and  saying  psalms  the 
whole  way ;  if  he  occasionally  spoke,  his  conversation 
was  always  upon  holy  things.  He  was  visited  by  the 
Archbishop  of  Urbino,  who  accompanied  him  to  Loreto, 
the  roads  by  which  they  went  being  full  of  pilgrims 
who  crowded  from  all  parts  to  see  him.  On  his  arrival 
in  the  evening  he  went  at  once  to  the  shrine,  and 
remained  there  all  night  in  prayer.  The  next  morning 
being  the  Nativity  of  our  Blessed  Lady,  one  of  the 
principal  feasts  there,  he  sang  Mass  and  preached  with 
such  fervour  on  the  love  of  God,  whose  only  begotten 
Son  had  taken  flesh  for  our  salvation  in  that  poor  little 
room  and  had  dwelt  there  in  poverty  and  humility 
many  years,  that  he  drew  tears  from  the  eyes  of  all 
present  He  gave  communion  to  many,  and  filled  the 
people  who  thronged  thither  with  no  small  degree  of 
wonder  and  edification,  every  one  thinking  there  was 
more  of  divine  than  human  in  him.  He  accepted  an 
invitation  of  the  canons  who  practised  community  life 
after  the  custom  of  early  times,  and  dined  with  them 
in  their  refectory. 

From  Loreto  he  went  on  to  Eome,  where  he  was 
looked  for  both  on  account  of  the  report  of  his  sanctity 
and  of  the  wonders  that  had  occurred  during  the 
plague  at  Milan.  Many  cardinals,  prelates,  and  nobles 
went  to  meet  him,  so  that  the  road  from  the  Porta  del 
Populo  to  the  Ponte  Molle  was  filled  with  crowds  of 
people.  It  was  most  striking  to  see  the  general  eager- 
ness manifested  to  do  honour  to  so  distinguished  a 
member  of  the  College  of  Cardinals.

CHAPTEK  II. 


THE  POPE'S  RECEPTION  OF  ST.    CHARLES  ARRIVAL  IN 

ROME  OF  ENVOYS  FROM  MILAN. 


On  his  arrival  in  the  city,  St.  Charles  alighted  at  his 
titular  house  of  St  Praxedes,  intending  to  visit  St. 
Peter's  and  the  Scala  Santa  the  first  thing  next  morn- 
ing. He  was  prevented  doing  so  by  the  Cardinals 
and  others  who  flocked  to  visit  him,  and  the  Pope, 
who  was  then  at  Frascati,  sent  a  special  messenger  to 
beg  him  to  take  np  his  abode  in  the  palace  of  the 
Cardinal  his  nephew  at  that  place.  This  request  of 
his  Holiness  not  only  gave  the  Cardinal  the  satisfac- 
tion of  being  admitted  to  his  presence,  but  also  the 
opportunity  of  speaking  upon  the  matters  which  had 
brought  him  to  Borne,  and  about  all  his  troubles, 
showing  how,  through  the  efforts  of  his  enemies,  all 
the  decrees  of  his  Fourth  Provincial  Council  had  been 
censured  by  those  who  had  been  deputed  to  revise 
them,  not  a  single  decree  having  been  left  as  it  stood. 
The  Pope,  knowing  the  goodness  of  his  intentions,  was 
beyond  measure  displeased  that  he  should  have  been

Sens,  one  of  the  congregation  of  revision,  who  showed 
him  a  packet  of  papers,  written  by  different  persons 
upon  this  subject.  The  Cardinal  was  then  given  to 
understand  that  there  was  no  foundation  for  these 
censures,  and  whence  all  the  opposition  had  arisen. 
Seeing  the  calumnies,  in  so  many  words,  he  said — "  I 
cannot  account  for  this ;  these  documents  cannot  be 
trusted.  Cardinal  Borromeo  is  a  member  of  our  col- 
lege, and  is  like  an  angel  from  heaven ;  it  would  be  a 
blessing  for  the  Holy  See  if  there  were  a  dozen  Car- 
dinals like  him.  I  have  an  only  nephew,  who  is  to 
start  to-morrow  morning  for  France,  whom  I  kept  here 
till  the  Cardinal  arrived  in  order  that  he  might  obtain 
his  blessing,  which  I  consider  will  be  of  great  service 
to  him." 

The  Pontiff  was  glad  to  hear  of  this  reply  of  the 
Cardinal  de  Sens,  and  to  see  the  deceits  of  Satan 


TJie  Popes  Reception  of  St.  Charles.  91 


brought  to  light.  With  apostolic  authority  he  con- 
firmed all  the  decrees  of  the  said  Council,  and  also 
those  of  the  Fifth,  which  the  saint  had  brought  with 
him.  He  also  invited  him  to  breakfast  at  his  table 
during  his  stay,  and  one  day  he  went  expressly  to  hear 
his  Mass,  and  see  his  vestments,  which  he  handled 
with  particular  devotion. 

St  Charles  then  returned  to  Rome  to  visit  the 
churches  and  holy  places,  the  Pope's  house  having  been 
during  those  eight  days  like  a  monastery,  all  striving 
to  keep  the  rules.  Cardinal  Guastavillani,  the  Pope's 
nephew,  even  directed  his  household  to  wear  the 
Borromean  livery  out  of  compliment  to  the  Saint 
Every  one  in  Eome  was  much  edified  by  his  humility ; 
two  of  the  Cardinals  who  had  not  known  him  well, 
but  had  been  set  against  him  by  others,  after  seeing 
him,  became  his  most  warm  friends.  His  enemies 
were  lowered  in  reputation  in  the  same  proportion,  as 
it  became  clear  that  they  had  been  moved  only  by  evil 
passions. 

He  received  much  kindness  from  his  brother  Car- 
dinals, and  used  to  invite  them  to  dine  with  him  at 
St  Praxedes,  having,  according  to  his  custom,  spiritual 
books  read  during  the  meal,  which  pleased  them  greatly 
on  account  of  the  benefit  they  derived  from  the  prac- 
tice ;  he,  on  the  other  hand,  relaxed  in  some  degree  his 
ordinary  rigour  and  abstinence  to  suit  himself  to  their 
way  of  living.  He  asked  to  his  table  also  many  other 
prelates  and  gentlemen,  striving  to  instil  into  them 
affections  for  spiritual  things,  and  to  incite  them  by 
his  discourse  to  devotion  and  piety,  setting  them  an 


92         Life  of  St.  Charles  Borromeo. 


example  himself  by  the  fervency  of  his  prayers,  and 
visits  to  the  churches,  whither  he  went  on  foot  He 
spent  the  whole  of  Christmas  night  in  watching  and 
prayer,  going,  after  the  midnight  Mass  at  St  Peter's, 
to  Santa  Maria  Maggiore,  where  he  remained  in  the 
Chapel  of  the  Manger  till  daybreak,  returning  thence 
to  St  Peter's  for  the  Pope's  Mass.  On  the  feast  of  St 
Sebastian  he  passed  the  whole  night  in  prayer  in  the 
subterranean  crypt  in  the  church  dedicated  to  that 
saint,  and  did  the  same  at  Tre  Fontane  in  the  church 
called  Scala  Coeli,  where  the  bodies  of  ten  thousand 
martyrs  repose. 

So  great  was  the  devotion  of  the  Roman  people  to 
him  that  they  rushed  out  to  see  him  as  he  passed 
through  the  streets,  and  many  knelt  down  to  show 
him  reverence ;  the  churches  were  filled  where  he  said 
Mass,  and  as  many  desired  to  receive  Holy  Communion 
from  him,  he  was  asked  by  the  Oratorian  Fathers  to 
officiate  at  a  general  Communion  in  the  Chiesa  Nuova, 
their  church.  Such  an  unusual  concourse  of  people 
came  together  that  an  account  of  it  was  printed,  with 
a  likeness  of  the  Cardinal.  He  was  asked  to  preach, 
but  declined  to  do  so  except  in  his  own  titular  church 
of  St.  Praxedes,  where  a  great  gathering  of  people 
went  to  hear  him,  many  of  the  nobility  of  both  sexes 
frequenting  the  church  in  order  to  receive  Communion 
at  his  hands,  although  it  was  at  some  distance  from 
the  city. 

During  this  sojourn  in  Rome  he  had  a  good  oppor- 
tunity of  doing  much  with  the  Pope  for  the  benefit  of 
the  whole  Church,  as  well  as  for  his  own  diocese  in 


Arrival  of  Envoys  from  Milan.  93 


particular.  He  obtained  the  revenue  of  the  Abbey  of 
Caiavaggio  for  his  Seminary,  and  that  of  St  Antony 
of  Pavia  for  the  Swiss  College.  The  Pope  was  quite 
satisfied  with  him,  finding  that  he  had  been  accused 
for  the  good  he  had  done ;  and  accordingly  approved 
by  word  of  mouth,  and  afterwards  by  writing,  of  all 
his  decrees  for  the  sanctification  of  festivals,  and 
against  profane  balls,  tournaments,  and  other  similar 
dissolute  amusements.  These  regulations,  indeed,  were 
so  pleasing  to  His  Holiness  that  he  was  wishful  to 
draw  up  a  general  constitution  or  code  of  them  for  all 
Christian  people,  but  for  some  particular  reasons  the 
project  was  not  carried  into  execution. 

St  Charles  on  this  occasion  urgently  appealed  for  a 
decision  on  the  controversies  about  jurisdiction,  for 
which  also  the  King  of  Spain  had  made  application 
through  the  Marquis  Alcagnizio,  who  was  at  Some 
for  the  purpose ;  but  as  it  was  an  affair  that  required 
time,  it  was  left  to  the  judgment  of  His  Holiness,  who, 
in  the  meantime,  availed  himself  much  of  his  advice  in 
important  matters,  to  the  great  benefit  and  advantage 
of  all  both  in  public  and  private.  The  Bishops  of 
Italy  especially  had  recourse  to  his  good  offices,  many 
coming  to  Some  for  the  purpose. 

While  the  Saint  was  engaged  in  this  way,  Satan  was 
not  idle  in  Milan,  for  being  in  doubt  whether  the 
servant  of  God  would  not  return  in  triumph  with  all 
his  decrees  confirmed  by  the  Pontiff,  he  made  it  his 
business  to  suggest  to  the  Governor  through  the  medium 
of  his  evil  counsellors  that  it  would  be  a  good  thing  to 
send  ambassadors  to  Some  to  oppose  the  Cardinal,  and 


94 


Life  of  St.  CJiarles  Borromeo. 


prevent  such  confirmation  if  possible,  otherwise  that 
the  Cardinal  would  be  sure  to  gain  the  day.  The 
Governor  called  together  the  Council  of  the  city,  pre- 
siding himself  as  grand  chancellor,  in  order  to  decide 
matters  according  to  his  own  will.  From  this  meeting 
were  absent  many  of  the  principal  decurions,1  and  those 
who  did  attend,  partly  from  interested  motives,  partly 
because  they  had  not  the  courage  to  make  any  opposi- 
tion, were  induced  to  elect  the  creatures  of  the  Gover- 
nor for  the  embassy,  one  of  whom  was  his  chief 
counsellor,  who  opposed  the  Cardinal  so  much.  When 
this  proceeding  was  made  known  it  caused  great  dis- 
pleasure in  the  whole  city,  as  every  one  took  it  ill  as 
being  unable  to  show  their  resentment.  The  people 
complained  that  their  city,  which  had  always  been 
most  loyal  to  their  archbishops,  should  now  be  compelled 
to  send  envoys  to  oppose  so  holy  a  pastor,  to  whom 
they  were  under  infinite  obligations.  The  Cardinal 
was  immediately  informed  of  these  measures,  and  re- 
ceived a  copy  of  the  letter  of  instructions  which  the 
ambassadors  were  taking  with  them.  He  was  deeply 
grieved,  not  on  his  own  account,  but  because  his  enemies 
allowed  themselves  to  be  so  blinded  by  their  passions, 
and  that  the  city  should  be  supposed  to  consent  to  an 
injustice  so  damaging  to  its  reputation ;  for  although 
in  nowise  blameworthy,  yet  the  report  of  what  had 
been  done  in  its  name  would  be  bruited  abroad. 

These  envoys  left  for  Eome  in  the  beginning  of  the 
year  1580,  causing  much  talk  throughout  the  country. 
A  rumour  was  spread  about  by  the  evil  disposed  that  the

Cardinal  would  not  return  again  to  Milan,  and  it  so 
far  gained  belief  that  even  in  Some  it  was  considered 
to  be  certain,  for  it  was  said  that  the  Pope  would  make 
him  Cardinal- Vicar.  On  being  asked  by  one  of  his 
household  if  this  report  were  true,  the  Saint  replied 
that  he  would  rather  resign  the  cardinalate  than  aban- 
don the  souls  which  God  had  committed  to  his  charge. 
Satan  thought  it  would  be  to  his  advantage  to  spread 
such  a  report,  but  as  some  good  religious  report,  the 
rumour  was  of  great  benefit  to  the  city  of  Rome,  for 
no  sooner  was  it  noised  abroad,  than  about  a  dozen 
notorious  courtesans  took  their  departure  without  wait- 
ing for  the  publication  of  a  decree,  so  high  was  his 
reputation  for  virtue  and  sanctity. 

The  Pope  in  the  meantime  had  gone  to  Palo  on  the 
sea  coast  where  he  sent  for  the  Saint,  who  wished  to 
give  His  Holiness  information  of  the  embassy,  to  make 
excuses  for  the  city  and  point  out  the  author  of  the 
mischief.  They  had  various  discussions  together  as 
to  the  best  way  of  receiving  and  dismissing  the  envoys. 
A  letter  was  written  to  them,  and  it  was  decided  that 
the  Cardinal  should  leave  Home  immediately  after  their 
arrival,  the  Pope  commissioning  him  to  pass  through 
Venice  to  conclude  important  business  with  that 
republic 

Before  leaving  Palo,  the  saint  wrote  to  Nicolas 
Galerio,  Canon  of  Padua,  his  vicar-general  at  Milan, 
to  have  the  edicts  again  published,  especially  those  on 
the  sanctification  of  festivals,  and  the  observance  of 
the  first  Sunday  of  Lent,  in  order  that  the  people 
might  not  think  they  had  been  suppressed,  and  that

Life  of  St.  Charles  Borromeo. 


they  were  at  liberty  to  renew  their  bacchanalian  dis- 
orders at  the  next  carnival. 

Hearing  of  the  arrival  of  the  envoys,  he  returned 
to  Borne  together  with  His  Holiness,  and  brought  his 
household  the  next  day  for  the  Pope's  blessing.  Having 
obtained  an  audience  for  the  ambassadors  at  the  same 
time,  he  introduced  them  himself  to  the  Pope,  explain- 
ing to  His  Holiness  the  high  position  they  held  in  the 
service  of  His  Catholic  Majesty.  With  the  Pope's 
blessing  he  then  retired,  leaving  them  at  liberty  to 
accomplish  their  mission  without  prejudice.  On  the 
next  day  there  was  a  consistory,  at  which  he  attended, 
and  there  took  leave  of  all  the  cardinals,  not  to  lose 
time  by  visiting  them  at  their  dwellings.  The  con- 
sistory being  ended,  he  rode  to  the  house  of  the  Cardinal 
of  Vercelli,  in  the  Borgo,  near  St  Peter's,  and  there 
received  the  visit  of  all  the  sacred  college,  and  of  the 
ambassadors  themselves,  who  were  displeased  at  his 
departure,  considering  that  it  was  a  slight  to  them- 
selves, when  another  would  have  stayed  to  defend 
himself.  They  prevailed  upon  the  Cardinal  of  Como 
and  Alciato  to  try  and  induce  him  to  remain,  saying 
that  he  appeared  to  have  little  consideration  for  the 
city  of  Milan,  which  they  represented,  the  more  so  as 
they  protested  that  they  desired  nothing  more  than 
the  accomplishment  of  his  wishes.  They  had  a  wily 
motive  in  saying  this,  in  order  to  detain  him,  that  by 
his  presence  in  Milan  he  might  not  prevent  a  relaxa- 
tion of  his  edicts,  which  they  had  planned  in  case  of 
his  absence ;  and  moreover,  because  they  had  boasted 
that  they  would  keep  him  in  Borne,  and  that  he  should 


Arrival  of  Envoys  from  Milan.  97 


never  go  back  to  Milan.  He  heard  this  request  with 
great  humility,  and  replied  that  he  had  great  affec- 
tion for  his  city,  that  he  wished  to  start  under  the 
circumstances,  leaving  them  more  at  liberty  for  their 
mission,'  that  he  would  offer  them  no  opposition,  but 
submit  entirely  to  the  decision  of  His  Holiness,  what- 
ever orders  he  might  give. 

The  poor  men  did  not  know  that  their  business 
had  been  already  considered  and  decided,  and  that 
they  were  to  receive  the  due  reward  of  their  presump- 
tion. "We  see  clearly  here  how  Satan  blinds  the  wise 
men  of  the  world  who  devote  themselves  to  politics 
without  piety  and  the  fear  of  God,  and  leads  them  to 
commit  egregious  mistakes  to  their  own  prejudice  and 
dishonour.  Such  was  the  case  of  these  envoys,  who 
became  a  byeword  among  the  people  under  the  name 
of  "  Carnival  ambassadors."  The  Saint  did  not  wish 
to  waste  time  in  discussion  with  them,  but  took  his 
leave  with  kind  words,  and  quitted  Rome  that  morning 
for  Venice.

CHAPTER  III. 

RETURN  BY  FLORENCE,  FERRARA,  AND  VENICE  TO  MILAN. 
I580. 

The  Saint  was  quite  as  much  honoured  on  his  de- 
parture as  he  had  been  on  his  entrance  into  Eome, 
being  accompanied  by  many  cardinals,  prelates,  and 
great  numbers  of  people  who  followed  in  sorrow  as  if 
their  father  was  leaving  them  taking  the  heart  of 
every  one  with  him.  When  he  reached  Florence,  he 
was  heartily  welcomed  by  the  Grand  Duke  Francis, 
who  considered  himself  as  his  son.  He  remained 
there  a  few  days  to  transact  important  business.  He 
was  compelled  to  satisfy  the  devotion  of  many  who 
wished  to  receive  communion,  which  he  gave  them  at 
the  Church  of  the  Jesuit  Fathers.  So  great  were  the 
numbers  that  he  had  difficulty  in  finishing  in  one 
morning.  He  praised  the  piety  of  the  Florentines,  but 
found  fault  with  the  fine  dresses  of  the  ladies. 

From  thence  he  went  to  Ferrara,  sending  his 
chamberlain  before  him,  in  order  not  to  take  the 
Duke  Alphonso  d'Este  by  surprise,  as  he  wished  to 
stay  a  short  time  there.  It  was  in  the  month  of 
February,  when  all  were  preparing  for  the  carnival ; 


Return  to  Milan. 


99 


but  the  Duke,  when  he  heard  that  the  Cardinal  was  on 
his  way,  withdrew  the  permission  which  he  had  given 
for  the  commencement  of  festivities,  and  forbade  all 
masking  and  other  pastimes  while  the  Cardinal  re- 
mained there.  He  then  went  to  meet  him,  and  received 
him  with  great  joy,  treating  him  as  a  royal  guest  during 
the  three  days  of  his  stay,  which  were  spent  by 
the  Saint  in  visits  to  the  churches,  in  preaching  and 
giving  communion  to  many  thousand  persons,  the 
duchess  herself  with  all  her  ladies  setting  the  example. 
All  were  astonished  to  see  such  a  change  all  at  once 
on  the  arrival  of  this  servant  of  God,  the  days  seem- 
ing like  those  in  Holy  Week. 

At  his  departure  for  Venice,  the  Duke  accompanied 
him  to  the  vessel  which  he  had  placed  at  his  disposal, 
secretly  ordering  another  to  follow  with  every  pre- 
paration and  provision  for  supper,  for  the  Cardinal 
was  sailing  by  night.  As  soon  as  he  discovered  it, 
knowing  that  many  of  the  Duke's  household  were  on 
board,  he  gave  orders  for  supper  to  be  served,  in  order 
not  to  take  them  any  further.  Early  in  the  morning 
he  reached  Chioggia  in  the  Venetian  territory,  where 
he  said  Mass  in  presence  of  the  whole  population.  He 
entered  Venice  privately,  alighting  at  the  house  of 
the  Papal  Nuncio.  He  had  hardly  arrived  when  the 
report  of  it  was  spread  throughout  the  city,  and  shortly 
came  the  Doge  in  the  Bucentaur,  accompanied  by  the 
senate,  to  visit  him,  in  especial  compliment  to  him. 
The  Venetian  Republic,  always  noted  for  its  splendid 
receptions,  seemed  determined  to  keep  up  its  reputa- 
tion for  magnificence,  receiving  him  in  grand  style,  and 


IOO 


Life  of  St.  Charles  Borromeo. 


supplying  him  with  everything  at  their  own  expense. 
During  the  nine  days  of  his  stay  he  had  more  than 
twenty  persons  at  his  table  every  day;  not  that  he 
liked  it,  but  because  he  did  not  wish  to  refuse  the 
favours  conferred  by  the  state,  and  knew  how  to 
accommodate  himself  to  all  times,  places,  and  circum- 
stances, and  to  reap  spiritual  gain  from  them.  Many 
of  the  principal  men  accompanied  him  to  visit  the 
Doge,  and  found,  to  their  astonishment,  that  all  the 
roads  were  crowded  with  people,  and  all  the  canals 
with  gondolas,  so  that  they  could  hardly  make  their 
way ;  he  could  scarcely  mount  the  stairs  of  the  palace 
for  the  multitudes  anxious  to  behold  him,  even  the 
roofs  being  crowded.  The  Doge  and  senate  welcomed 
him  with  honour  and  affection,  and  then  withdrew 
to  treat  of  the  business  of  his  commission  from  the 
Pontiff.  The  complimentary  visits  required  by  his 
rank  and  position  being  over,  he  went  to  visit  the 
churches  and  sacred  relics,  in  which  the  city  abounded, 
and  was  presented  with  some  of  great  value,  which 
he  took  with  him  to  Milan. 

There  were  in  Venice  at  this  time  about  sixteen 
bishops  and  church  dignitaries,  who,  although  they  did 
not  before  appear  in  clerical  attire,  now  were  all  seen 
as  bishops  and  prelates  in  the  proper  habit  of  their 
rank,  the  people  being  greatly  surprised  at  so  unusual 
a  sight,  remarking  that  so  many  priests  had  never 
been  seen  in  Venice  before,  as  hitherto  they  had  not 
been  publicly  known  as  such.  He  particularly  urged 
the  clergy  of  the  city  and  a  congregation  of  regulars 
who  have  a  college  there  to  adopt  the  square  clerical 


Return,  to  Milan. 


ior 


berretta  instead  of  the  round  one.  The  bishops  he 
exhorted  to  reside  at  their  sees  and  not  to  absent 
themselves  without  good  reason,  and  he  asked  the 
Holy  Father  to  send  orders  to  that  effect.  By  request 
he  gave  general  communion  at  the  Jesuit  church,  and 
preached  at  the  wish  of  the  Patriarch  and  Apostolic 
Nuncio ;  and  although  it  was  the  Thursday  after  Sexa- 
gesima  Sunday,  commonly  called  "Giovedi  grasso,"  the 
crowding  of  the  churches  was  so  great  that  it  seemed 
like  Easter  Day,  not  a  single  person  being  seen  with  a 
mask  in  public. 

When  invited  to  visit  the  arsenal,  he  at  first  de- 
clined, considering  it  a  mere  matter  of  curiosity  and  a 
loss  of  time,  but  on  being  shown  the  inscription  over 
the  entrance,  "  For  the  defence  of  the  Catholic  faith," 
and  told  that  it  ought  to  be  seen  by  every  pious  per- 
son, he  gave  way  and  went  over  the  whole  place,  being 
pleased  to  see  such  a  store  of  arms  and  ammunition. 

As  he  had  proposed  to  make  a  visitation  of  Brescia, 
a  city  in  the  dominions  of  Venice,  he  asked  the 
authorities  to  forward  his  wishes,  which  they  were 
glad  to  do.  From  the  willingness  of  the  Venetians  to 
give  up  their  worldly  amusements,  in  order  to  attend 
to  piety  and  devotion  during  the  few  days  he  had  been  , 
in  their  city,  he  anticipated  great  benefit  would  arise 
from  an  Episcopal  visitation,  and  wrote  strongly  to 
His  Holiness,  asking  him  to  send  thither  the  Bishop 
of  Verona,  Augustine  Valerio,  after  he  had  finished 
the  visitation  of  Dalmatia. 

He  took  his  departure  from  Venice  on  the  eve 
of  Quinquagesima   Sunday,  accompanied  by  many

dignitaries,  among  whom  was  the  Bishop  of  Padua, 
Frederick  Cornaro,  afterwards  Cardinal,  with  whom  he 
stopped  the  following  day,  preaching  in  his  cathedral, 
and  giving  communion  to  a  great  number  of  persons. 

From  Padua  he  went  on  to  Vicenza,  where  he  was 
met  by  the  Bishop  and  inhabitants,  who  begged  him 
to  stay  till  the  following  day,  which  was  Tuesday,  the 
day  of  the  carnival,  in  order  that  they  might  all  make 
a  spiritual  carnival  by  going  to  confession  and  com- 
munion. He  entreated  them  to  excuse  him,  as  he  had 
to  be  at  Milan  on  the  following  Saturday  to  keep  the 
first  Sunday  of  Lent  there,  promising  them  that  at 
Mass  on  the  morrow  lie  would  give  them  a  discourse, 
and  communion  to  all  who  were  prepared  for  it.  The 
priests  had  to  remain  in  the  confessionals  all  night 
hearing  the  confessions  of  the  people,  who  filled  the 
cathedral  in  the  morning  to  hear  his  Mass  and  sermon 
and  to  go  to  communion,  seeming  entirely  to  forget 
that  it  was  carnival  day. 

As  his  friend  the  Bishop  of  Verona  was  still  absent 
on  his  visitation  in  Dalmatia,  he  determined  to  pro- 
ceed without  stopping  there,  as  he  was  pressed  for 
time.  But  a  prelate  who  saw  him  passing  through, 
went  in  haste  to  the  gate  to  warn  the  soldiers  on 
guard  to  raise  the  drawbridge  and  not  allow  Cardinal 
Borromeo  to  pass  over.  To  the  Saint's  entreaties  to 
be  allowed  to  pass  that  evening,  it  being  about  five 
o'clock,  the  porter  replied  that  he  had  orders  not  to 
open  it  to  any  one  under  pain  of  death.  In  the  mean- 
time the  lords  of  the  city  and  a  great  concourse  of 
people  came  with  complaints  at  his  hurrying  away  so

quickly,  without  blessing  the  city  by  his  presence. 
Although  he  made  many  apologies,  and  begged  to  be 
allowed  to  continue  his  journey,  they  would  not  yield, 
so  that  he  was  obliged  to  go  back  and  stay  at  the 
Bishop's  house.  So  great  was  the  delight  of  the 
people  when  they  heard  of  his  consent,  that  it  quite 
drove  from  their  minds  the  carnival  in  which  they 
had  all  been  occupied  shortly  before.  The  next  day 
being  Ash  Wednesday,  he  said  Mass  before  daybreak, 
and  gave  the  blessed  ashes  to  the  people ;  and  as  it 
was  still  dark  when  he  finished,  he  was  escorted  out 
of  the  city  on  the  road  to  Brescia  by  torchlight. 

The  Brescians  being  apprised  of  his  coming,  wel-

bishop of  the  province.  He  stayed  three  days  to 
make  arrangements  for  the  visitation  of  the  city  and 
diocese  which  he  wished  to  hold  shortly.  Here  he 
began  to  hear  the  voices  of  his  beloved  Milanese,  who 
were  impatiently  expecting  him,  notwithstanding  the 
false  reports  of  his  enemies  as  to  his  never  again 
returning.  He  had  no  sooner  passed  Martinengo  than 
he  met  many  of  his  flock  who  had  set  out  to  meet 

him. 

There  was  a  still  greater  demonstration  in  the  even- 
ing at  Triviglio,  where  he  passed  the  night ;  for  all  the 
inhabitants  rushed  out  to  see  him,  tears  falling  from 
their  eyes  for  joy,  the  church  bells  being  rung  as  if 
for  a  festival. .  When  he  left  in  the  morning,  all  the 
people  accompanied  him  on  the  way,  praising  God  for 
his  happy  return. 

When  he  reached  Pozzolo,  twelve  miles  from  Milan, 


104        Life  of  St.  Cliarles  Borromeo. 

he  found  entire  confraternities  and  schools  meeting 
him  in  procession ;  the  nearer  he  came  to  the  city,  the 
greater  was  the  concourse,  so  that  he  was  obliged  to 
go  slowly  for  the  crowds— every  one  seeking  to  touch 
his  garments,  his  boots,  or  his  mule,  tears  flowing  from 
all  eyes  so  abundantly  that  they  would  have  melted  a 
stone ;  for  the  people,  not  being  able  to  express  their 
joy,  made  their  eyes  supply  the  defect  of  their  tongues. 
It  was  considered  wonderful  that  his  mule,  at  other 
times  so  restive,  seemed  then  to  sympathise  with  the 
people,  letting  them  touch  and  press  against  him  with- 
out kicking.  Among  the  rest  was  a  lady  who  went 
out  two  miles  to  meet  him,  who  no  sooner  saw  him 
than,  forgetting  decorum  and  the  danger  to  which  she 
was  exposed,  cast  herself  at  the  mule's  feet,  sobbing 
aloud  out  of  the  fulness  of  her  heart.  Seeing  these 
extraordinary  marks  of  affection,  the  Saint  could  scarcely 
refrain  himself  from  tears. 

As  he  approached  the  city  gates  all  the  bells  of  the 
churches  rang  out  as  a  sign  of  his  arrival,  and  men 
and  women,  old  and  young,  of  every  condition,  went 
forth  to  meet  him.  The  streets  were  soon  so  full  of 
people  that  they  crushed  and  stifled  one  another,  not 
without  damage  to  the  shopkeepers,  who  could  not  keep 
them  off,  not  even  with  naked  weapons. 

The  saint  had  great  difficulty  in  reaching  the  cathe- 
dral, and  much  more  in  getting  to  his  own  house. 
Tears  were  shed  in  floods,  and  voices  were  heard  cry- 
ing, "  Our  Cardinal  is  come,  who  was  never  to  return, 
as  they  said ;  it  is  not  true  that  the  Pope  has  made 
him  bis  Vicar-General  at  Eome;  we  shall  hear  his

CHAPTER  IV. 


EVENTS  AT  MIL  AX :  DISMISSAL  OF  THE  MILANESE  ENVOYS 
BY  THE  POPE. 

I580. 

It  must  not  be  supposed  that  St.  Charles  was  allowed 
by  Satan  to  remain  long  at  peace,  God  suffering  it  to 
be  so,  lest  public  applause  should  give  rise  to  self- 
complacency,  and  that  continual  mortification  might 
lift  him  to  a  higher  degree  of  sanctity.  As  the  envoys 
met  with  delays  in  Eome,  in  order  to  assert  their  claims 
more  vigorously,  and  to  show  that  the  decrees  were 
not  accepted  in  Milan,  letters  were  despatched  by  them 
to  the  Governor,  begging  him  to  order  the  festivities 
and  tournaments  as  usual  on  the  first  Sunday  of  Lent 
in  order  to  assert  their  rights.  The  Governor  accord- 
ingly invited  many  knights  and  gentlemen  of  the  city 
to  take  part  in  them,  feeling  sure  of  having  an  im- 
posing celebration.  Among  the  Milanese,  however, 
who  had  been  extremely  displeased  at  the  embassy 
sent  to  Eome,  no  one  could  be  found  to  transgress  the 
orders  of  the  Cardinal,  or  again  to  profane  the  Sunday. 
The  Governor,  in  order  to  avoid  the  shame  of  a  defeat, 
and  to  carry  out  the  request  of  the  ambassadors,  ordered

one  of  the  captains  to  bring  up  his  company  from  Pavia, 
where  they  were  in  garrison,  to  tilt  in  the  games.  This 
was  done  in  spite  of  the  penalty  of  excommunication 
incurred  ipso  facto,  as  before  mentioned. 

"When  the  Saint  on  his  arrival  heard  of  the  Gover- 
nor's preparations,  he  directed  that  the  usual  general 
communion  should  be  announced  in  the  cathedral  and 
other  churches  of  the  city,  in  order  to  gain  the  plenary 
indulgence.  He  was  himself  in  the  church  at  an  early 
hour,  and  having  said  Mass,  gave  communion  to  the 
people,  and  did  not  finish  till  two  o'clock  in  the  day ; 
though  he  was  assisted  by  the  canons  who  gave  com- 
munion at  different  altars,  he  could  scarcely  satisfy  the 
multitude,  and  would  willingly  have  continued  till  night- 
fall had  he  not  been  obliged  to  stop  short  to  sing  Vespers. 
The  communion  being  ended  without  any  rest,  he  sang 
Pontifical  High  Mass,  and  then  ascended  the  pulpit 
to  preach,  the  people  thronging  the  cathedral  to  over- 
flowing. 

In  that  address,  which  was  the  most  earnest  I  ever 
heard  from  him,  he  was  particularly  affected  on  giving 
the  people  the  blessing  of  the  Supreme  Pontiff,  first 
explaining  the  importance  of  the  benediction  of  the 
Vicar  of  Christ,  and  in  bestowing  it  he  made  use  of 
the  words  of  Moses  in  blessing  the  people  of  Israel  in 
God's  name :  "  Blessed  shalt  thou  be  in  the  city,  and 
blessed  shalt  thou  be  in  the  field," 1  &c,  which  he 
uttered  with  such  feeling  that  no  one  could  refrain 
from  tears. 

But  in  the  square  outside,  combatants  in  masks

were  incurring  the  penalties  of  the  Church  in  the  pre-

moment  trumpets  sounded  so  loudly  that  they  echoed

I  was  present  at  the  time,  and  afraid  that  this  uproar 
would  disconcert  him,  narrowly  watched  him ;  but  he

without  leaving  it,  thronged  as  it  was  all  day  long. 

This  incident  wounded  liim  to  see  how  little  heed 
was  paid  to  the  censures  of  the  Church,  purposely 
defied  to  the  scandal  of  the  public,  to  God's  dishonour, 
and  to  the  destruction  of  those  poor  souls  who  in  the 
hardness  of  their  hearts  were  publicly  encouraged  to 
incur  them.  He  was  more  deeply  pained,  as  the  evil 
was  prompted  by  one  who  ought  to  have  worked  with 
him  and  aided  in  the  spiritual  government  of  a  state 
whose  King  was  so  zealous  for  the  salvation  of  his 
subjects.  Holding  the  place  of  God  as  pastor,  he  felt 
compelled  to  take  measures  to  prevent  such  scandalous 
excesses  in  future,  and  accordingly  after  due  consulta- 
tion he  denounced,  by  word  of  mouth  and  writing,  all 
those  who  had  taken  part  in  the  tournaments  or  had 
ordered  or  encouraged  them,  as  well  as  those  who  had 
been  present  at  them,  and  forbade  them  to  enter  the 
churches,  that  all  who  had  committed  so  grievous  a 
sin  should  be  anxious  to  free  themselves  from  the 
censures  they  had  incurred.  The  result  was  that 
those  who  had  been  induced  to  be  present  at  the

tilting-match,  and  among  them  some  of  the  Governor's

There  was  a  Spanish  Capuchin  monk,  Father  Lupo, 
preaching  at  that  time  in  the  cathedral,  who  reproved 
the  Governor  in  private,  aud  exhorted  him  to  consider 
how  grievous  a  sin  it  was  to  despise  the  prelates  of 
the  Church  and  treat  their  censures  with  disdain,  as 
the  source  of  every  evil,  of  heresies,  and  the  ruin  of 
kingdoms.  In  a  sermon  he  publicly  denounced  this 
sin,  and  reproved  those  confessors  who,  in  order  to 
gain  the  favour  of  princes,  foster  their  evil  intentions 
though  contrary  to  ecclesiastical  discipline.  "  If  those 
religious,"  he  said,  "  who  have  the  direction  of  con- 
sciences, possess  the  Spirit  of  God  and  would  obey 
their  chief  pastors  all  would  be  well,  and  we  should 
not  see  such  scandals  among  Christian  people  as  we 
behold  nowadays  ;  for  they  would  then  strive  to  keep 
men  united  in  loyalty  to  their  rulers  and  obedient  to 
their  commands.11 

I  remember  that  when  this  zealous  Father  ended

his  reproof,  he  said  that  his  habit  and  profession  bound 
him  to  speak  the  truth,  and  that  if  he  should  be  beaten 
to  death  for  it  as  soon  as  he  left  the  pulpit,  he  should 
consider  it  the  greatest  gain  he  could  receive  in 
this  life.  His  words  produced  a  good  effect,  for  the 
prisoners  were  immediately  released;  and  the  Apos-

absolved  from  the  censures ;  which  was  all  their  pastor 
desired,  viz.,  to  lead  men  to  acknowledge  their  sins  and 
amend  their  lives.  However,  this  did  not  save  the  captain

the  Church ;  for,  being  within  a  few  months  thrown  into 
prisou  for  certain  misdeeds,  he  found  means  of  escaping 
to  Lugano  in  the  Swiss  territory,  and  there  was  un- 
fortunately murdered — a  warning  to  all  to  reverence 
their  pastors  and  take  heed  to  their  censures. 

In  the  meantime  the  ambassadors  in  Borne  were 
making  every  effort  to  obtain  a  decision  in  their  favour ; 
but  His  Holiness  proceeded  with  circumspection,  con- 
sulting persons  of  experience,  and  noting  down  with 
his  own  hand  the  reasons  and  replies  that  inclined 
him  to  sanction  the  Cardinal's  decrees,  which  finally 
as  Vicar  of  God  he  approved  and  confirmed  as  to 
be  observed  by  all  This  answer  displeased  the 
ambassadors,  who  found  themselves  disappointed  in 
their  hopes  and  obliged  to  go  back  in  disgrace.  They 
uttered  loud  complaints,  saying  that  the  Milanese 
ought  not  to  be  forced  more  than  any  others  to  obey 
laws  that  were  not  observed  elsewhere,  not  even  in 
Rome  itself.  The  Pope  paid  no  attention  to  these 
murmurs,  except  that  in  Eome  he  prohibited  the  custom

"Pope  Gregory  XIII. — Beloved  children,  health 
and  the  apostolic  blessing.  From  your  letters  received 
at  different  times,  and  from  the  statement  of  your  am-

thee  shall  see  me/  says  the  Prophet;  and  this  joy 
will  bring  you  to  share  in  the  same  crown  as  your 
pastor,  according  to  the  promise  of  God  to  Abraham : 
'  I  will  bless  those  who  bless  thee,  and  I  will  curse 
those  who  curse  thee.' 

"  Although  your  opinion  and  that  of  all  good  men 
gives  us  no  reason  to  suppose  that  your  pastor  would 
make  any  order  contrary  to  right  and  justice,  yet  we 
take  in  good  part  the  complaints  you  bring  before  us, 
and  commend  you  for  informing  us  of  them  and  sub- 
mitting them  to  our  judgment  as  children  devoted  to 
this  see  and  beloved  by  us.

"  In  compliance  with  your  request,  having  examined 
with  the  greatest  care  all  the  questions  propounded, 
we  consider  that  the  observance  of  the  decrees  will  be 
of  great  benefit  to  you,  and  we  exhort  you  to  obey 
them  with  a  ready  mind,  not  only  refraining  from 
opposing  them  in  any  way,  but  with  all  your  power 
aiding  to  carry  them  into  execution,  as  we  have 
explained  to  the  Cardinal  himself.  We  are  aware 
that  they  may  appear  somewhat  hard  at  first,  but  with 
good  will,  which  every  one  should  pray  with  con- 
fidence to  obtain  from  God,  they  will  become  sweet 
and  easy.  Xarrow  and  strait  is  the  way  to  Leaven 
when  we  look  at  our  fallen  nature,  but  in  the  grace  of 
God  the  yoke  of  the  Lord  is  easy.  When  habit  is 
joined  to  a  willing  mind,  those  things  will  be  found 
light  which  at  first  seemed  heavy.  Above  all,  the 
great  charity  of  your  pastor  ought  to  console  you,  who 
only  looks  to  the  salvation  of  the  flock  committed  to 
him  by  God,  valuing  it  more  than  his  own  life,  as  you 
have  clearly  seen.  Place  yourselves,  therefore,  in  his 
hands,  which  you  have  found  in  times  of  danger  ever 
ready  to  be  employed  for  your  salvation,  disposing 
yourselves  to  obedience  to  a  pastor  who  loves  you  so 
much,  and  be  assured  that  in  so  doing  you  are  fulfill- 
ing your  duty  and  acting  in  a  manner  most  pleasing  to 
God,  and  will  enjoy  that  peace  of  Christ  our  Lord 
which  we  all  so  earnestly  desire." 

The  ambassadors,  knowing  the  tenor  of  this  brief, 
would  not  present  it  themselves  for  very  shame:  it 
was  sent  by  other  means,  and  was  not  opened  till  the 
year  1602,  when  it  was  placed  in  the  hands  of  Mgr.

lished throughout  the  city  to  the  great  joy  of  all  who 
had  been  displeased  by  the  doings  of  the  Envoys1  who 
had  brought  reproach  upon  the  city  without  fault  of 
its  own. 

We  may  see  in  thi3  way  how  the  wiles  of  Satan  are 
defeated  by  the  hand  of  God,  and  that  although  He 
permits  tribulations  to  fall  upon  His  servants,  yet 
in  the  end  He  makes  known  to  all  their  sanctity. 
Wretched  are  those  who,  blinded  by  the  same  devices, 
are  led  to  persecute  their  pastors  who  serve  God  with 
all  their  hearts ;  they  end  their  lives  miserably,  and 
leave  behind  them  but  a  sorry  memory.  Happy,  on 
the  contrary,  will  be  those  bishops  and  pastors  of  souls 
who  do  not  lose  heart  amid  difficulties  and  opposition 
in  reforming  their  flocks ;  for  those  who  labour  with  a 
right  intention  are  never  abandoned  by  God. 

1  The  two  enroyi,  or  "carniral  ambassadors,"  were  Count  Pietro 
Antonio  Lonato  and  Camfllo  Trotto,  both  creatures  of  Ayaxnonte.

CHAPTER  V. 


VISITATION  OF  TOE  DIOCESE  OF  BRESCIA,  DEATH  OF  THE 
GOVERNOR  OF  MILAN,  SEVENTH  DIOCESAN  SYNOD. 


After  the  beginning  of  Lent,  St.  Charles  returned  to 
Brescia  to  begin  his  visitation.  He  took  with  him 
but  eight  assistants,  in  order  not  to  lay  too  heavy  a 
burden  upon  the  city.  The  people  made  great  pre- 
parations to  receive  him,  having  raised  triumphal 
arches  and  decorated  the  streets  with  royal  magni- 
ficence. JBe  was  welcomed  by  the  Bishop  and  clergy, 
together  with  the  nobility  and  people  of  the  city, 
with  such  demonstrations  of  universal  joy  as  testified 
the  delight  of  the  citizens.  The  Saint  began  with  a 
solemn  High  Mass  in  the  cathedral,  when  he  explained 
to  the  people  the  object  and  importance  of  the  visita- 
tion, entreating  all  to  strive  to  obtain  due  benefit  from 
it,  and  gave  communion  to  great  numbers  of  people, 
finishing  the  visitation  in  Holy  Week.  He  went  back 
to  Milan  for  Palm  Sunday  and  Easter  Day,  and  at 
that  time  paid  a  visit  to  the  Governor,  hoping  it  might 
be  productive  of  benefit  to  him  by  leading  him  to 
acknowledge  his  wrongdoings  in  the  matter  of  the

Visits  the  Diocese  of  Brescia.         1 1 5 


ecclesiastical  censures,  so  great  was  his  desire  to  save 
his  souL  It  seemed  that  the  Governor  was  troubled 
at  this  exhortation,  for  raising  his  eyes  to  heaven,  "  It 
is  too  much,"  he  said,  "to  require  of  the  Milanese  what 
is  not  done  elsewhere  ? "  thus  showing  what  a  bad 
impression  had  been  made  upon  his  mind,  that  he 
should  be  so  indisposed  to  obedience.  Yet  as  the 
lieutenant  of  the  Catholic  king, — who  was  so  desirous 
that  all  his  subjects  should  fear  God  as  good  Chris-

son, — he  ought  to  have  been  glad  to  aid  the  Arch- 
bishop in  banishing  abuses  which  led  to  many  sins 
and  in  helping  men  along  the  road  to  heaven. 

The  Governor  thanked  the  Cardinal  for  his  paternal 
admonitions,  and  paid  him  more  honour  than  usual 
at  his  departure,  as  if  he  had  a  presentiment  that  this 
would  be  his  last  visit ;  for  he  shortly  afterwards  had 
an  attack  of  fever,  which  carried  him  off  in  a  few  days, 
at  the  time  the  Saint  was  on  his  way  to  Brescia. 
Learning  that  he  was  on  his  deathbed,  the  Cardinal 
returned  with  all  speed  and  found  him  in  his  agony, 
breathing  with  great  difficulty,  as  if  he  could  not 
die.  His  struggles  ceased,  to  the  astonishment  of 
the  bystanders,  with  the  arrival  of  the  Cardinal,  who 
assisted  him  to  make  a  good  death,  and  afterwards 
said  Mass  for  the  repose  of  his  soul,  and  accompanied 
his  body  to  the  grave,  preaching  upon  death  and  the 
wretched  condition  of  human  things. 

Before  he  went  back  to  Brescia  he  held  his  seventh 
diocesan  synod  on  the  20th  of  April,  and  though  it 
lasted  three  days  as  usual,  there  were  no  decrees  made,

but  those  of  the  fourth  and  fifth  Provincial  Councils 
were  read  which  he  had  brought  with  the  Papal  con-

four  sermons  to  the  clergy,  a  perfect  compendium  of

He  then  spent  some  time  in  continuing  his  visita- 
tion of  Brescia,  as  it  was  a  large  and  populous  diocese, 
but  was  frequently  interrupted  by  other  business  to 
which  he  had  to  attend ;  he  was  not  in  consequence 
able  to  finish  it  until  the  following  year,  1581.  He 
first  visited  the  city,  banishing  all  abuses  and  bad 
customs,  and  introducing  a  wholesome  reform  in  dis- 
cipline, which  he  did  not  find  difficult  on  account 
of  the  good-will  of  the  people,  who  were  so  devoted 
to  him  that  they  gladly  obeyed  his  slightest  wish. 
Wherever  he  went,  he  was  followed  by  great  numbers 
of  people,  some  kissing  his  garments,  others  touching 
him  with  their  rosaries  as  is  the  custom  with  the  relics 
of  the  saints. 

His  fatigue  was  great  in  giving  communion,  both  on 
account  of  the  devotion  of  the  people  and  a  plenary 
indulgence  granted  at  the  time,  there  being  as  great 
a  concourse  as  at  the  season  of  a  jubilee. 

Discovering  that  there  were  in  the  Castle  of  Brescia 
the  bodies  of  four  sainted  bishops,  and  that  of  St 
Dominator  in  particular,  which  were  not  receiving  the

honour  due  to  them,  as  access  to  the  fortress  was  not

cathedral  in  accordance  with  the  wish  of  the  people. 
Permission  was  asked  of  the  government  at  Venice, 
where  there  was  a  long  discussion  of  the  subject ;  and

made  the  translation  with  great  solemnity  to  the 
cathedral,  where  the  people  could  more  conveniently 
have  recourse  to  their  intercession. 

He  also  endeavoured  to  settle  the  question  of  the 
relics  of  SS.  Faustinus  and  Jovita,  martyrs  and  pro- 
tectors of  the  city,  in  order  to  put  an  end  to  a  con-

the  possession  of  them  for  their  church.  The  cause 
was  tried,  but  as  it  took  much  time,  was  not  decided ; 
however,  the  relics  are  supposed  to  be  preserved  in 
the  church  of  the  Cassinese  congregation  of  Benedic- 
tines. 

This  diocese  includes  the  important  valley  called 
Camonica,  extending  to  the  confines  of  the  territory  of 
the  Grisons,  many  parts  of  which,  being  wild  and 
uncultivated,  are  difficult  of  access,  and  in  a  bad  state 
as  regards  morals  and  the  worship  of  God.  The  clergy 
especially  observed  no  discipline,  and  set  a  very  bad 
example,  sorely  needing  correction.  But  the  Venetian 
rulers  doubted  whether  the  Saint's  visit  might  not  lead 
to  disturbances,  the  inhabitants  being  so  ill-disposed. 
They  therefore  wrote  to  the  Pope,  begging  him  to 
desire  the  Cardinal  not  to  visit  the  valley  himself, 


I  iS        Life  of  St.  Cliarles  Borromeo. 


but  to  send  some  prelate  from  their  own  dominion. 
His  Holiness  replied  that  as  the  Cardinal  had  great 
prudence,  he  left  it  to  his  decision.  St  Charles,  know- 
ing the  state  of  the  valley,  where,  on  account  of  the 
neighbourhood  of  heretics,  greater  freedom  was  allowed 
from  fear  of  insurrection,  decided  not  only  to  visit  the 
district  himself,  but  to  spend  some  time  there,  in  order 
that  he  might  be  able  to  do  more  good  among  those 
poor  souls.  Making  his  visitation,  therefore,  in  the 
spirit  of  compassion,  he  endeavoured  to  show  the 
clergy  and  people  how  little  their  lives  were  conformed 
to  the  laws  of  the  gospel,  and  that  the  churches  were 
not  treated  with  the  respect  due  to  the  houses  of  God. 
So  great  was  the  efficacy  of  his  words  in  addition  to 
the  holiness  of  his  life,  that  a  general  conversion  took 
place ;  all  his  decrees  were  obeyed,  and  the  sacraments 
received  with  such  devotion  that  he  often  said  he 
never  had  greater  consolation.  They  strewed  his  path 
with  flowers  to  show  the  love  they  bore  him,  and  he 
had  such  influence  among  them,  that  many  of  the 
clergy  who  had  grown  old  in  open  concubinage  and 
other  sins,  which  from  custom  were  thought  nothing 
of  by  the  people,  came  freely  to  his  feet  to  disclose 
their  wounds,  determined  to  save  their  souls.  The 
Saint  willingly  received  them  with  these  signs  of  true 
amendment,  and  absolved  them  from  these  grievous 
sins.  Such  cases  were  so  frequent  that  the  Cardinal, 
astonished  at  the  confidence  they  placed  in  him,  asked 
them  what  had  moved  them  to  confess  their  iniquities, 
of  which  he  had  no  knowledge.  "  We  desire,"  they 
said.  "  to  change  our  lives  and  to  be  reconciled  to  God,

A  remarkable  circumstance  happened  as  he  was

prelate  was  an  eloquent  preacher :  his  sermon  had 
such  an  effect  upon  the  people  that  they  paid  the 
tithes,  and  the  Bishop  freed  them  from  the  interdict 

The  Cardinal  stopped  there  on  his  return  to  say

CHAPTER  VI. 


LABOURS  IX  THE  VALTELLIXE :  STATE  OF  THE  CATHOLIC

Ix  the  Grison  district,  bordering  on  the  Camonica 
valley,  is  the  Valtelline,  where  there  is  a  church 
dedicated  to  our  Blessed  Lady,  called  Santa  Maria  of 
Tirano,  a  place  of  great  resort  in  those  parts,  a  con- 
tinual concourse  of  the  faithful  flocking  thither  from 
distant  parts  on  account  of  the  graces  received  from 
God  through  the  intercession  of  His  Holy  Mother. 

St  Charles,  having  great  devotion  to  our  Lady, 
resolved  to  visit  this  church  as  it  was  only  fifteen 
miles  distant.  He  wished  at  the  same  time  to  make 
a  visitation  of  the  district,  which  was  much  infected 
with  the  heresy  of  Calvin,  in  order  to  try  what  he 
could  do  to  root  it  out,  and  to  make  the  way  easy  for 
the  Bishop  of  Como,  to  whose  diocese  it  belongs.  He 
had  spoken  on  the  subject  to  the  Supreme  Pontiff, 
and  had  therefore  full  authorisation.  The  people  of 
Tirano,  hearing  that  he  was  travelling  in  those  parts, 
sent  envoys  to  beg  that  he  would  by  no  means  fail  to 
visit  them,  and  to  favour  them  with  a  discourse,  assur-
